I deem it expedient, further to impress a due obedience to the abovementioued Royal Ordinance that it may in future be a guidance to all concerned. The principal points are these : þÿ Sec. 1 That Children who are to be made members of either of the above congregations, shall be baptized, in either of the respective Churches, in the Islands of St. Croix and St. Thomas, within 8 Weeks after their birth, and iu the Island o! St Johns within 4 Months. Sec. 2. That baptism, as a holy rite ought to be performed by the Minister of the Gospel and in the house of God, provided proof has not been adduced, that the life of the child, through illness, might be in danger of being carried to church, in which case, the baptism may be performed at home ; and should such illness continue until the child attains the age mentioned in Section 1, it nevertheless becomes a duty to have it baptised at home. Sec. 3. That the private (or home.) baptism, shall always be performed by eiiher of the respec-

tive Ministers, unless that the life of the In fant should be in immediate danger, and that the services of the former can not be obtained, then and in that case, the baptism mav be performed by a protestaut Minister, one of the Brethren of the Moravian sect or congregation, or any other ordained person, a Schoolmaster, or a well informed Christian of proper age and moral conduct, consequently the baptism may be performed by the child's father, but no midwife or any other female is permited to officiate, unless that the feeble slate of the child, connected with other circumstances, may prevent the obtaining in due time, the assistance of a male, endowed with the abovementioned qualities to perform the baptism. Sec. 4. Should the time ordained bv Law, having expired, for the baptism of the child, the Minister is then bound to remind the father, and if an illegitimate child, the mother, to obey the mandate or the Law, and if those concerned, do not at the very first Sunday of service, after such warning, conform with their duty, such obliquity of conduct, must immediately becommunicated by the Minister, to the Royal Westindia Government of St. Croix and to the Royal Council in St. Thomas, who will strictly enjoin the concerned, to have the child christened the following sundav of service, subject to a fine from 1 to 5 ps. |). From the Barbadian, October 14, 1837. ACCOUNT OF THE CREW OF THE SHIP STIRRING CASTLE, AND THE BARBAROUS CONDUCT OF THE SAVAGES.

(From þÿBell Weekly s Messenger, August 20.) (Concluded from our last.) Two days after this horrible event, a fine looking young man, named James Major, was disposed of, Captain Frazer, who knew a good deal of the character and habits of the savages on this coast, had mentioned to Major that the savages would take off his head for a figure bust for one of their canoes. It seemed, too, that it was usual for the savage who contemplated that sort of execution, to smile in the face of his victim immediately before he struck him to the earth. While Major was at work the chief of his tribe approached him smiling, and tapped him on the shoulder. At that instant the poor fellow received a blow on the back of the neck from a waddir or crooked stick, which stunned him. lie fell to the ground, and a couple of savages set to work, and by means of sharpened shells severed the head from the body with frightful lacerations. They then ate j>a its of the body, and preserved the head with certain gums of extraordinary efficacy, and affixed it as a figure bust to one of their canoes. The rest of the crew of course expected nothing less than death. Their apprehensions appeared to relate rather to the mode of inflicting the extreme penalty, than to the fact that they must prematurely die. þÿ Two of the seamen, named Doyle and Big Ben, contrived to steal a canoe, and endeavoured to cross an inland lake, but were drowned in the attempt to escape from, perhaps, a more painful death. There was a black man named Joseph,

who had been steward on board the Stirling Castle, when the savages seized the long boat, in which the crew had entered White Bav ; they stripped this Joseph as well as the rest, but as he was of their own colour they inflicted no punishment upon him ; and he had the privilege of going about, which was denied to any other of the wretched strangers. This man, who was constantly watching for an opportunity to escape, had assured Mrs. Frazer that if he could get away the first life he should think of saving should be that of his misstress. He succeeded in stealing a canoe, in which he rowed off, and in six weeks he reached Moreton Bay, where he informed the commandant of the penal settlement of the horrible circumstances which had taken place at White Bay, and of the servitude in which the survivors of the crew were detained. By this time Mrs. Frazer was separated, and at a considerable distance from the different members of the crew, and she .had given up all hopes of ever being liberated from this frightful bondage in which she was detained. The Moreton Bay commandant, on hearing of the affair, inquired in the barracks whether any of the military would volunteer to save a lady and several of 'the crew of the wrecked vessel from the savages in the bush, and a number offered their services at a moment s notice. By a svstem of manoeuvring entered into by a convict who had been for some years in the bush, amongst the savages, the object was effected. All the þÿsurvivors were, to the best of Mrs. þÿFrazer b s elief, res-
cued from the savages,

BASTSK TESTSinttSK At the camp the commandant and the company, and, in fact, all the individuals who were In the service of the government, treat, ed Mrs. Frazer and her companions in misfortune with a degree of kindness which it is evident she will ever have a very warm recolfection of. She was placed under medical care immediately, and every thing was done that was considered likely to abate the sense of what she had undergone in witnessing the murder of her husband, and the other horrors with which she had been surrounded. The captain of the Mediterranean packet in which Mrs Frazer arrived from Sydney at Liverpool, stated that he was at Sydney at the time of the arrival of that lady, and that the circumstances detailed caused the greatest excitement there. The convict to whose extraordinary return Mrs. blazer owed her escape, obtained a free pardon from the government there, and a reward of thirty guineas. The Lord Mayor asked what were the circumstances of Mrs Frazer. He was convinced, that it she was in necessity, the ladies in London, who were constantly looking for such objects, would speedily relieve her. The captain said that the unfortunate lady was not misstress of a farthing. The clothes on her back, had been given to her fry the commandant's wife, and Captain Frazer had been the sole support of her and three children, who were in the Orkney Islands, to which she was anxious to go as soon as possible. She was lame, and had almost lost the use of one arm, and the sight of one eye,

by the severity of the inflictions to which she had been subjected. þÿ You know the history of the big ship, Congress having appropriated eight millions of dollais to build a certain number of seventy-fours, there happened to be left a surplus o! about $800,000, and this sum was appropriated to the building of a crack ship, which would do honor to American naval architecture, and to the flag she was to bear. She was accordingly built and housed very snugly until Dr. Sutherland, with a zeal which did him honor, urged Congress to have her completed and launched, that she might be seen by foreign nations, and be an evidence of the power, the taste, and the skill of our country. The Navy yard in this city and this ship in particular, have long been preeminent lions ; no stranger ever passed through Philadelphia without visiting the Navy-yard, which for many years has been under the charge of the veteran Barron. He recently threw up the command of the yard, in consequence of being under the orders of his junior officers, w ho are commissioners of that most useless of all bureaus, the Navy Commissioners Board, and whose duties have always clashed with the head of the Department, producing embarrassments and difficulties which have long thrown our Navy in the back ground. Commodore Stewart, however, commanded, and made the most judicious arrangements to secure safety to all concerned in the no small tasks of launching a ship

Sailors with their blue jackets and tarpuhn hats ; dutch girls from the country with nosegays and short petticoats ; ladies of fashion in their carriages and barouches ; gentlemen on horseback, and dandies with their canes and moustaches, on foot ; mechanics and labourers with their wives and daughters, all well dressed and well behaved, were journeying towards the navy yard, which was sur rounded with tables with fruit, refreshments of all kinds, olvcooks and pretzels. The river Delaware, which at this point is rather narrow shelly and shallow, was filled with steamboats j and small craft of all kinds, and the flags and steamers, and concourse of people, and bands of music, lent animation to the scene. It was computed and I think with reason, that 100,000 persons were present, and nearly thi ee hundred persons on board the large ship admitted as 1 understand, by cards According to arrangements and with the view of all the small craft getting out of the way of danger, two guns were fired a litlie after two o'clock. Then commenced the movements on the þÿw aters ; the steam-boats whizzed past ; the little wherries scudded by ; the pilot boats luffed up and bore away; it was like the roll of the drum and the shouts on the race grounds, þÿ clearthe þÿcourse. It was all clear; a broad path was made for the þÿ monster þÿ; the clink of hammers was soon heard

knocking up the wedges, and about half past two þÿo clock the cry was þÿ there she þÿgoes. And sure enough she did go glancing like a swan into the water, and throwing up the waves to the right and left, and rocking the big and little barks like cradles on the deep. It was all over; she was safe ; and those who þÿ took the þÿresponsibility, felt light and happy that they could report þÿ all is þÿwell. þÿ The people went home quietly and contentedly ; it was a glorious sight and they enjoyed it. From the 1'rovidcnce Mornihg Courier. THE TEST OF BENEVOLENCE. a short am) true story. " The lianrl that wiped away that tear of want, The heart that melted at another's woe, Were his, and blessings followed him " David Went worth had the kindest of hearts. There was neither mete nor bound to his benevolence, except inability. And happy was any inan who had a tythe of the prayers that were offered up for the welfare of my friend, by the unfortunate and wretched whom his band had relieved. I speak of prayers þÿ for it was the only reward ho sought, and of course the only reward he obtained ; I mean here þÿ but I forgot. David was paying attention to an excellent young lady of his native city. She was wealthy, beautiful, accomplished, and consequently had many suitors. Among them were richer and nobler (in extraction I mean) and handsomer than David, but n'importe there was a kind of frank hearted, straight forwardness about my friend, that could not fail to carry him somewhere near the heart of his discerning mistress, even if an emperor had been his rival.

The young lady in question, hit upon a project to put the characters of her lovers to a test. She had come across a poor widow with a family in distress in one of her benevolent excursions, and the idea occurred to her that it would be a good opportunity to ascertain the stuff her lover's heart was made of. þÿ Letters were forihwith indited, setting forth the good woman's tale, and forwarded to the different gentlemen in the widow's name, requesting an answer and assistance. The first reply was a lecture on idleness and begging, and concluded with the information that the writer was not accustomed to give to those lie did not know. This was from $ 1 0,000 a year þÿ1 The second advised her to apply to some of the benevolent societies whose duty it was to relieve those who were truly in want. This was from one who had a great reputation for benevolence þÿ who had taken a leading part in several chaiitable associations; and whose pharasaical liberality hud been blazoned in the Gazette. The lady thought that interested, as he w as, in the success of these institutions, he displayed very a commendable reluctance about taking the business out of their hands A lint d from a good hearted and generous kind of a fellow þÿ enclosed her a $5 bill with his coniplinitnts- Several took no notice ol the good woman's petition. But there vvas another answer which the lady read with far different feelings. It was from David from StNitO a year and þÿ þÿ 1 need not say, like himself kmu and consoling.

It spoke of the writer's narrow means, and also « : the principles he lias adopted, of never giving, unless persuaded of the worthiness of the otiject, and concluded Liv requesting an interview. " If," said he, " 1 find myself otherwise unable to afford the assistance you require, I trust I may he of service in interesting others in your behalf." Nor was this profession. For it was but a few weeks before the widow found herself comfortable located and engaged in a thriving little business, commenced by the recommendation, and carried on by the aid of a friend. And all this was done in genuine scripture style. There was no sounding of trumpets ; and the right hand knew not tin. doings of the left. But his lady-love vvas a silent observer of his conduct, and fie received many a kind glance from that quarter, of which he little suspected the cause. She begun to think that a homage of a spit it like his w as a thing not to be despised : and she felt something very much like a palpitation of the li'art, as she questioned lie, self respecting Ins intention. She was in a train of thought which was one evening, as is often the case, interrupted by a call liom the very person who had been its cause. Hour after Itour passed by tbut nigbt, and still David lingered He could not tear himself away, " She is a most lascinai ig creature," thought he, " and good us she is bcautilul. Can she ever lie mine /" A cloud came over his features and he sat for u moment in silence. " This suspense must be

ended," he at length thought ile started as Hie clock told eleven. " You will certainly think me insufferably tedious, said lie, with a feint smile, but 1 " have been so pleasantly engaged as to think no more of time. And the sin of this trespass upon the rules of good breeding must lie at your door. Besides, 1 have lengthened this visit," he continued after a pause, "under the apprehension that as it has been the happiest, it might also he the last, it shall ever bo my good fortune to enjoy with Mist ii."

The lady looked at him with some surprise. " Nay," said he, " the n atter rests with yourself. Will you forgive my presumption ? 1 know that others perhaps more worthy of you, at least nobler and wealthier and higher in the world's esteem, arc striving for the honor of your hand. And yet 1 cannot lestrain myself from making an avowal, which, though it may he futile, it is yet but a deserved tribute to your worth." And he popped the question. The lady did not swoon nor turn pale. þÿ But a flash of gratification passed over her face, and lighted her eyes for a moment. She frankly gave him her hand and looked up archly in his face. 1' The friend of the fatherless and widow,'' said she, (David blushed) " cannot fail to make a constant lover und a worthy husband ."

THE ISLAND OF ST. CKOIX. Little is known of this Island by the public generally as a resort for Invalids ; it not haviug been much frequented by them until lat lerly, owing to a want ot the boarding houses now established, though the reputation of the dimate for the relief and cure of chronic diseases has long been known to many. Hav ing been more than once a sojourner in that beautiful spot, or highly cultivated garden as it is very justly termed, the writer has tiad the opportunity of benefiting with many of his countrymen by its mild and sulubrious climate ; and is therefore desirous of making it more extensively known. In the first place it is not to be understood that all Invalids wdio go there are restored to health ; þÿ on the contrary, some are not suffered to return. But, we would ask, was not all hope of the recovery of th sc unfomnaie individuals abandoned by their fi -mis and medical advisers before they left then homes and did not many of them survive bevond the :r expectations ! Were no: their sufferings less acute, their dis? on more gradual in that climate, th n uid have been the case in ours? Uut of about 200 of our countrymen who were at St. Croix during the past winter, there were twenty deaihs. With a few exceptions these cases were considered utterly hopeless on their arrival, and the writer solemnly believes lie would have been spaicd the pains of recording these exceptions, if proper care and advice had been taken. What have invalids and convalescents to

do with fatiguing walks and rides in a West India sun t We heard of an invalid Gentleman who walked from Basin to West End, a distance of sixteen miles bv way of a mornþÿing s exercise to give relish and zest to his breakfast, and of a lady in delicate health, who rode the same distance for the same commendable purpose. þÿl say o nothing of the risks incurred by sail, ing, fishing, and marooning excursions. The writer must not be understood t-> object to exercise and cheerful society for the recovery oflost health As good air and proper food, lie considers them indispensably- necessary to that object, þÿ but in every climate they must be taken with caution and judgment, more particularly in a tropical one. In the next place it is not to be supposed that persons cannot get sink there. This remark is made in consequence of the thoughtlessness with which individuals have been known te expose themselves; who on reflection would not have done the same at home. We will venture to say, that with proper caution and care, where the climate injures one, it benefits a thousand. The last winter had not been as favorable as usual ; so the inhabi tants told us, and yve believe it from our experience of former ones owing no doubt to the heavy rains during the preceding fall, and an unusual prevalence of northerly þÿwinds. These causes often produce fever and ague among some of the inhabitants, in a greater or less degree, according to the situation of their residences, or the exposure they subject
themselves to. Strangers are not as likelv to be attacked by fever and ague as residents are, though there were several cases of it last winter among them, produced by the same causes.

It has been before stated, that there were 200 of our countrymen at St. Croix during the last winter. Of this number strike ofl one fourth who accompanied their invalid friends, leaving 150 all more or less afflicted with pulmonary complaints. þÿ Out of this number> some have entirely recovered, some are convalescent, some may yet be spared to their friends for a time, and 20 have died. Hoyv many more deaths would probably have occurred had these individuals remained at home, and how many yvho are now well and convalescent, yvould be in a deep and settled decline ! This is a cheerful view of the sub- ; ject, and speaks volumes in favor of the Island as a resort for invalids. We yvould not recommend our countrymen to wait until they are invalided. We would cry yvith a stentorian voice, to all who have the least evidence of a consumptive symptom, þÿ Go> and go at once, or you may defer it until too þÿlate. To those yvho wish to flee from the chilling blasts of winter, vve can recommend it as a safe and delightful retreat. The climate nas been already spoken of, although in terms far short of its merits. To know it properly, one must have felt its soft and balmy air, stealing imperceptibly over the senses, lulling pain and care by its kind and general influences þÿ In no season that we have been there, has the glass on our premises been lower than t4 degrees or higher than S3 degrees Fahrenheit from the months of November to May. Until this season it had not been loyver than 65

degrees. At no period had there been a greater variation than 5 degrees in 24 hours, and this yve found very unosuai þÿ 2 or 3 degrees not being uncommon, though we have observed the mercury to stand at 75 to 76 for several days in succession, and this we should judge to be about the standard during those months. What does not this say in comparison to our climate where a change of 50 degrees is not uncommon in 24 hours.

The houses generally, are constructed for air and coolness, consequently they ate very open, and many of them without glass sashes iu tnc windows A draught of air should al- Ways be carefully avoided, though we confess in some houses this is not a little difficult mat-

, The English in the Island, and the society intelligent and I ct- iivated, the yvealthier members thereof I Having been educated abroad. Of their kindness and hospitality we can speak most favorably. as can most of our countrymen. þÿ We did meet with some exceptions, but soon learnt the cause of it. þÿi eople who go abroad determined to find fault with every body they meet and everything they see, had much better stay at home, or if they must needs go, should be shut up by themselves. They are not satisfied with making every body and every thing disagreeable to themselves, hut endeavour to make them equally so to others. 1 he more you endeavour to please such folks, the more you irritate them, and it is decidedly the best plan to let them alone. A gentleman or lady will soon be known in any intelligent community, and in no place sooner than St. Croix. '1 he roads ! what shall he said of them, a few words will suffice þÿ the wide world affords no better. As a general thing we would not tccoinmend taking a horse or carriage, as there are many now in the l&lund that cun he hired,

though should the influx of strangers next year be great, as we have no doubt it will or ought to be, there would be difficulty in serving all. Ponies can be hired for $12 per month or thereabouts. It may bo asked which part of the Island is preferable. We give the choice decidedly to Basin as the coolest of the two, and in the estimation of the inhabitants generally less subject to fevers than the West End. There is a very romantic road near West End that surpasses any at Bassin side. With the exception of this, we thought the roads equally pleasant about Bassin, and in one respect greatly preferable, namely, the absence of limestone soil, which gives a white glare to the roads in and about West End, and it is painful to the eyes when the sun shines. There are some excellent houses established in both towns and vicinities, and the price of board is from $10 to 12 per week. All the precious metals of the United States are taken at the same value as with us ; as also Mexican Dollars. Col. and Sp. Doubloons are worth $16. We should recommend remittances to be forwarded in preference to drawing bills, and every one who can conj veniently, had better provide himself with a | passport. We would suggest plenty of light j clothing with the exception of coats for invalid gentlemen, and no one should neglect to take his stock of flannel and wear it. We have somewhere heard of a þÿpainter s quaint idea of representing the Goddess Hyegea as holding a pair of flannel inexpressibles

in one hand ; to complete the picture, we would suggest that a flannel waistcoat be painted in the other also. Before closing these remarks, it would he necessary to caution individuals against leaving the island too early in the spring Many leave it as early as April, which is too soon, as some have discovered to their sorrow, The month of June would he the proper time, and quite early enough to come on our coast with safety after spending six months in such a climate. We cannot recommend leaving early for a southern city; there is too great a risk and uncertain! v in doing this. During the last season the ship Emilv left for Savannah about the middle of April, and on arriving there found nine inches ol snow on the ground. We were told that sumc of her passengers would have returned language is universally spoken j j ed a day or two earlier than she expected. to St. Croix with the vessel, had she not sail- When the good work of convalescence has commenced, all who can possibly stay until it is completed, should do so. It often proves the shortest way in the end, and it is attended with less risk and expense. If any remam through the summer, they should select cool and airy situations, with well ventilated rooms. There are some situations where vve could have fancied to remain, did not other obstacles prevent, and vve have no doubt this will become common hereafter. We area restless, impatient nation, and often injure ourselves irremediably by these causes. þÿ Hardly allowing ourselves time to eat, much

less do we think we cun spare the time and means necessary to resuscitate a delicate and worn out constitution Nothing but dear bought experience will teach us. G. B. » mt srjura j A GOOD (i room cV Coachman , jtlcnsc apply to the þÿI INTER. ll Christiaiisted 18th Sept. 1 887.

MESSAGE FROM THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES To the two Houses of Congress at the commencement of the first session oj the Twentyfifth Congress. Fellow Citizens of the Senate and House of Representatives The act of the 23d of June, 1830, regulating the depsites of the public money, and directing the employment of State, District, and Territorial Banks for that purpose, made it the duly of the Secretary of the Treasury to discontinue the use of such of them as should at any time refuse to redeem their notes in specie, and to substitute other banks, provided a sufficient number could be obtained to receive the public deposits upon the terms and conditions therein prescribed. The general and almost simultaneous suspension of specie payments by the banks in May last, rendered the performance of this duty imperative, in respect to those which had been selected under the act ; and made it, at the same time, impracticable employ to the requisite number of others, upon the prescribed conditions. þÿ The specific regulations established by Congress for the depositeand safe keeping of the public moneys, having thus unexpectedly become inoperative, 1 feel it to be my duty to afford you an early opportunity for the exercise of your supervisory powers over the subject. I was also led to apprehend that the suspension of specie payments, increasing the embarrassments before existing in the pecu niary affairs of the country, would so far diminish the public revenue, that the accruing

receipts into the Treasury, would not, with the reserved five millions, be sufficient to defray the unavoidable expenses of ihe Government, until the usual period for the meeting of Congress; whilst the authority to call upon the States, for portion a of the sums deposited with them, was too restricted to enable the Department to realize a sufficient amount from that source. These apprehensions have been justified by subsequent results, which render it certain that this deficencv will occur, if additional means be not provided by Congress. The difficulties experienced by the mercantile interest, in meeting their engagements, induced them to apply to me, previously to the actual suspension of specie payments, for indulgence upon their bonds for duties, and all the relief authorized by law was promptly and cheerfully granted. The dependence of the Treasury upon the avails of these bonds, to enable it to make the deposites with the States required by law, led me in the outset to limit this indulgence to the first of September, but it has since been extended to the first of October, that the matter might be submitted to your further direction. Questions were also expected to arise in the recess in respect to the October instalment of those deposites requiring the interposition of Congress. A provision of another act, passed about the same time, and intended to secure a faithful compliance wilh the obligation of the United States, to satisfy all demands upon them

in specie or its equivalent, prohibited the oiler of any bank note, not convertible on the spot into gold or silver at the will of the holder ; and the ability of the Government, with millions on deposite, to meet its engagements in the manner thus required by law, was rendered very doubtful by the event to which 1 have referred. Sensible that adequate provisions for these unexpected exigencies could only be made by Congress ; convinced that some of them would lie indispensably necessary to the public service, before there regular period of your meeting ; and desirous, also, to enable you to exercise, at the earliest moment, your full constitutional powers for the relief of the country, could not, with propriety, avoid subjecting you to the inconvenience of assembling at as early a day as the state of the popular repre-

sentation would permit. I am sure that I have done but justice to your feelings, in believing that this inconvenience will be cheerfully encountered, in the liopeof rendering your meeting conducive to the good of the country. During the earlier stages of the revolution through which we have just passed, much acrimonious discussion arose, and great diversity of opinion existed, as to its real causes. This was not surprising. The operations of credit are so deversified, and the influences which affect them so numerous, and often so subtle, that even impartial and W'ellinformed persons are seldom found to agree in respect to them. To inherent difficulties were also added other tendencies, which were by no means favorable to the discovery of truth, it was hardly to be expected, that those who disapproved the policy of the Government in relation to the currency, would, in the excited state of the public feeling, produced by the occasion, fail to attribute to that policy any extensive embarrassment in the monetary affairs of the country. The matter thus became connected with the passions and conflicts of party ; opinions were more or less affected by political considerations, and differences were prolonged which might other- I wise have been determined by an appeal to facts by the exercise of reason, or by mutual j concession. It is however, a cheering reflection, that circumstances of this nature cannot prevent a community so intelligent as ours from ultimately arriving at correct conclu-

sions. Encouraged by the firm belief of this truth, I proceed to state my views, so far as may be necessary to a clear understanding j of the remedies 1 feel it my duty to propose, and of the reasons by which 1 have been led to recommend them. The history of trade in the United States for the last three or four years affords the most convincing evidence that our present condition is chiefly to be attributed to overaction in all the departments of business; an over-action, derived, perhaps, its first impulses from antecedent causes, but stimulated to its destructive consequences by excessive issues of bank paper, and by other facilities for the acquisition and enlargement of credit. At the commencement of the year 1834, the banking capital of the U. States, including that of the National Bank, then existing, amounted to about two hundred millions of dollars ; the bank notes then in circulation to about ninetv-five millions; and the loans and discounts of the banks to about three hundred and twenty-four millions. Between that time and the first of January, 183(5, being the latest period to which accurate accounts have been received, our banking capital was increased | to more than two hundred and fifty-one mil- j lions ; our paper circulation to more than one hundred and forty millions, and the loans and discounts to more than lour hundred and fiftyseven millions. To this vast increase are to be added the many millions of credit, acquir- \ ed by means of foreign loans contracted by i

the States and State Institutions, and above all, by the lavish accommodations extended j by foreign dealers to our merchants. The consequences of the redundancy of credit and of the spirit of reckless speculation engendered by it, were a foreign debt con- j traded by our citizens, estimated in March | last at more than thirty millions of dollars ; the extension to tradefs in the interior of our country of credits for supplies, greatly beyond the wants of the people; the investment of thirty-nine and a hall millions of dollars in unproductive public lands, in the year 1835 and 183(5, whilst in the preceding year the sales amounted to only four and a half millions ; the creation of debts, to an almost countless amount, for real estate in existing or anticipated cities and villages, equally unproductive, and at prices now seen to have been greatly disproportionate to their real value ; the expenditure of immense sums in improvements which, in many cases, have I been found to be ruinously improvident ; the I diversion to other pursuits of much of the labor that should have been applied to agriculture, thereby contributing to the expenditure of large sums in the importation of grain from Europe þÿ an expenditure which, amounting in 1834 to about two hundred and fifty thou-

þÿwm þÿnegaraw sand dollars, was, in the two first quarters of the present year, increas þÿ d to more than two millions of dollars ; and. finally, without enumerating other injurious results, the rapid growth among all classes, and especially in our great commercial towns, of luxurious habits, founded too often on merely fancied wealth, anil detrimental alike to the industry, the resources, and the moruls of our people. It was so impossible that such a state of things could long continue, that the prospect of revulsion w as present to the minds of considerate men before it actually came. None, however, had correctly anticipated its severity. A concurrence of circumstances inadequate of themselves to produce such widespread and calamitous embarrassments, tended so greatly to aggravate them, that they were overlooked in considering their history. Among those to be mentioned, as most prominent, the great loss of capital sustained by our commercial emporium m the fire of December þÿ1835 a loss, the effects of which were underated at the time, because postponed for a season by the great facilities of credit then existing; the disturbing effects, in our commercial cities, of the transfers of the public moneys required by the deposite law of June, 183(5; and the measures adopted bv the foreign creditors of our merchants to reduce their debts, and to withdraw from the United States a large portion of our specie. However unwilling.any of our citizens may heretofore have been to assign to these causes

the chief instrumentality in producing the present state of things, the developments subsequently made, and the actual condition of other commercial countries, must, as it seems to me, dispel all remaining doubts upon the subject. It has since appeared that evils, similar to those suffered by ourselves, have been experienced in Great Britain, |on the continent, and, indeed, throughout the commercial world; and that in other countries, as well as in our own, they have been uniformly preceded by an undue enlargement of the boundaries of trade, prompted, as v»ith us, by unprecedented expansions of the systems of credit. A reference to the amount of banking capital, and the issues of paper credits put in circulation in Great Britain, by banks and in other wavs, during the years 1834, 1835, and 183(5, wifi show an augmentation of the paper currency there, as much dispronorlioned to the real wants of trade as in the United States. W ith this redundancy of the paper currency, there arose in that country also a spirit of adventurous speculation, embracing the whole range of human enterprise. Aid was profusely given to projected improvements ; large investments were made in foreign stocks and loans; credits for goods were granted with unbounded liberality to merchants in foreign countries ; and till the means of acquiring and employing credit were put in active operation, ami extended in their effects to every departmant of business, and to every quarter of the globe. þÿ

The re action was proportioned in its violence to the extraordinary chaiacterof the events wdiich preceded it. The commercial community of Grert Britain were subjected to the greatest difficulties, and their debtors in this country were not only suddenly deprived of accustomed and expected credits, hut called upon for payments, which, in the actual posture of things here, could only be made through a general pressure, and at the most ruinous sacrifices. In view of these facts, it would seem impossible for sincere inquiries after truth, to resist the conviction, that the causes of the revulsion in both countries have been substantially the same. Two nations, the most commercial in the world, enjoying but recently the highest degree of apparent prosperity, and maintaining with each other the closest relations, are suddenly, in a time of profound peace, and without any great national disaster, arrested in their career, and plunged into a state of embarrassment and distress. In both countries we have witnessed the same redundancy of paper money and other facilities of credit; the same spirit of speculation ; the same partial successes ; the same difficulties a,|d reverses ; and, at length, nearly the same overw helming catastrophe. The most material difference between the results in the

þÿiuu.;i < two countries lias only been, that with us there has also occurred an extensive derangement in the fiscal affairs of the Federal and State Governments, occasioned by the suspension of specie payments by the banks. The history of these causes and effects, in Great Britain and the United States, is sub stautially the history of the revulsion in all other commercial countries. The present, and visible effects of these circumstances on the operations of the Government and on the industry of the people, point out the objects which call for your immediate attention. They are þÿ to regulate by law the safe keeping, transfer, and disbursement, of the public moneys ; to designate the funds to be received and paid by the Government ; to enable the Treasury to meet promptly every demand upon it ; to prescribe the terms of indulgence, and the mode of settlement to be adopted, as well in collecting from individuals the revenue that has accrued, as in withdrawing it from former depositories, and to devise and adopt such further measures, within the constitutional competency of Congress as vvill be best calculated to revive the enterprise and to promote the prosperity of the country. For the deposite, tranfer, and disbursement of the revenue, National and Slate banks have always, with temporary and limited exceptions, been heretofore employed ; but, although advocates of each system are still to be found, it is apparent that the events of the last, few months have greatly augmented the

desire, long existing among the people of the United States, to separate the fiscal operations of the Government from those of individuals or corporations. Again to create a national bank, as a fiscal agent, would be to disregard the popular will, twice solemnly and unequivocally expressed. On no question of domestic policy is there stronger evidence that the sentiments of a large majority are deliberately fixed ; and I cannot concur with those who think they see, in recent events, a proof that these sentiments are, or a reason that they should be changed. Events, similar in their origin and character have heretofore frequently occurred, without producing any such change ; and the lessons of experience must he forgotten, if we suppose the present overthrow of credit would have been prevented by the existence of a national bank. Proneness to excessive issues have ever been the vice of the banking system; a vice as prominent in National as in State Institutions This propensity is as subservient to the advancement of private interests in the one as in the other : and those who direct them both, being principally guided by the same views, and influenced by the same motives, vvill be equally ready to stimulate extravagance of enterprise by improvidence ol credit. How strikingly is this conclusion sustained by experience. The Bank of the United Stales with the vast powers conferred on it by congress, did not or could not prevent former similar embarassments ; nor has the

still greater strength it has been said to possess, under its present charter, enabled it, in the existing emergency, to check other institutions, or even to save itself. In Great Britain, vvltere it lias been seen, the same causes have been attended witli the same effects, a national bank, possessing powers tar greater than arc asked for by the warmest advocates of such an institution here, has also proved unable to prevent an undue expansion of credit, and the evils that flow from it. Nor can 1 find any tenable ground for the re-establislimeut of a national bank, in the (derangement alleged at present to exist in the domestic changes of tiic country, or in the facilities it may be capable of affording them. Although advantages of this sort were anticipated when tin; first Bank of the United States was created, they were regarded as an incidental accommodation ; not one which the Federal Government was bound, or could be called upon, to furnish. This accommodation is now, indeed, alter the lupse of not many years, demanded from it as among its first duties ; and an omission to aid and regulate commercial

exchange, is treated as a ground of loud and serious complaint. Such results only serve to exemplify the constant desire among some of our citizens, to enlarge the powers of the Government, ami extend its control to subjects with which it should not interfere. þÿ They can never justify the creation of an institution to promote such objects. On the contrary, they justly excite among the community a more diligent inquiry into the character of those operations of trade, towards which it is desired to extend such peculiar favors. The various transactions which bear the name of domestic exchanges, differ essentially in their nature, operation & utility. One lass of them consists of bills of exchange, drawn for the purpose of transferring actual capital from one part of the country to another, or to anticipate the proceeds of property actually transmitted. Bills of this description are highly useful in the movements of trade, and well deserve all the encouragement which can rightfully he given to them. Another class is made up of bills of exchange, not drawn to transfer actual capital, nor on the credit of property transmitted, but to create fictitous capital, partaking at once of the character of notes discounted in bank, and of bank notes in circulation, and swelling the mass of paper credits to a vast extent in the most objectionable manner. These bills have formed, for the last few years, large propor- a tion of what are termed the domestic exchanges of the country, serving as the means

of usurious profit, and constituting the most unsafe and precarious paper in circulation.'þÿ This species of traffic, instead of being upheld, ought to be discountenanced by the Government and the people. In transferring its funds from place to place, the Government is on the same footing with the private citizens, and may resort to the same legal means. It may do so through the medium of bills drawn by itself, or purchased from others ; and in these operations it may in a manner undoubtedly constitutional and legitimate, facilitate and assist exchanges ol individuals, founded on real transactions of trade. The extent to which this may be done, and the best means of affecting it, are entitled to the fullest consideration. This has been bestowed by the Secretary of the Treasury, and bis views will be submitted to you in his report. But it was not designed bv the Constitution that the Government should assume the management of domestic or foreign exchange. It is indeed authorised to regulate by law the commerce between the States, and to provide a general standard of value, or medium of exchange, in gold and silver ; but it is not its province to aid individuals, in the transfer of their funds, otherwise than through the facilities afforded by the Post Office Department, As justly might it be called on to provide for the transportation of their merchandize. þÿ These are operations of trade. They ought to be conducted by those who are interested in them, in the same manner that the inciden-

tal difficulties attending other pursuits are encountered by other classes of citizens þÿ Such aid lias not been deemed necessary in other countries. Throughout Europe, the domestic, as well as the foreign exchanges, are carried on by private houses, often, if not generally without the assistance of banks- þÿ Vet they extend throughout distinct sovereignties, and far exceed in amount the real exchanges of the United States There is no reason why our own may not be conducted in the same manner, with equal cheapness and safety. Certainly this might he accomplished, if it were favoured by those most deeply interested ; and few the their own interest, as well as can doubt that general welfare of the country, would he promoted by leaving such a subjeci in the hands ol those to whom it properly belongs. A system founded on private interest, enterprise and competition, without the aid of legislative grants or regulations by law, would rapidly of it would be free from the influence prosper ; political agitation, and extend the same exemption to trade itself; and it would put an end to those complaints of neglect, partiality, injustice, and oppression, which are the unavoida-

ble results of interference hv the Government in the proper concerns of individuals. Ail former attempts on the part ot the Government to carry its legislation, in this respect, further than was designed by the Constitution, have in the end proved injurious, and have served only to convince the great body ol the people, more and more, of the certain dangers of blending private interests with the operations of public business ; and there is no reason to suppose that a repetition of them now would be more successful. It cannot he concealed that there exists, in our community, opinions and feelings on this subject in direct opposition to each other. þÿ A large portion them, combining great of intelligence, activity, and influence, are no doubt sincere in their belief that the operations of trade ought to be assisted by such a connection ; they regard a national bank as necessary for this purpose, and they are disinclined to every measure that does not tend, sooner or later, to the establishment ol such an institution On the other hand, a majority of the people are believed to be irreconcilably opposed to that measure ; they consider such a concentration of power dangerous to their liberties : and many of them regard it as a violation of the Constitution. This collision of opinion has, doubtless, caused much of the embarassment to which the commercial transactions of the country have lately been exposed. Banking has become a political topic of the highest interest, and trade has suffered

in the conflict of parties. A speedy tei mi nation of this state of things, however desirable, is scarcely to be expected. We have seen for nearly half a century, that those who advocate a national bank, by whatever motive they may be influenced, constitute a portion of our community too numerous to allow us to hope for an early abandonment of their favorite plan. On the other hand, they must indeed form an erroneous estimate of the intelligence and temper of the American people, who suppose that they have continued, on slight or insufficient grounds, their presevering opposition to such an institution ; or that they can be induced by pecuniary pressure or by any other combination of circumstances, to surrender principles they have so long and so inflexible maintained. My own views of the subject are unchanged. They have been repeatedly & unreservedly announced to my fellow citizens ; who, with full knowledge of them, conferred upon me the two highest offices of the government. On the Inst of these occasions, 1 felt it due to the people to apprize them distinctly, that, in the event of mv election, I would not he able to co operate in the re-establishment of a national bank. To the«e sentiments I have now only to add, the expression of an increased conviction, that the re-establishment of such a hank, in any form, w hilst it would not accomplish the beneficial purpose promised by its advocates, would impair the rightful supremacy of the popular will; injure the char-

acter and diminish the influence of our political system ; and bring once more into existence a concentrated moneyed power, hostile to the spirit, and threatening the permanency, of our republican institutions (To he continued.)

Local banks have been employed for the deposite and distribution of the revenue, at all times partially, and, on three different occasions, exclusively ; first, anterior to the j establishment of the first Bank of the United States; secondly, in the interval between the termination of that institution and the charter of its successor ; and, thirdly, during the limited period which has so abruptly closed. The connection thus repeatedly attempted, proved unsatisfactory on each successive occasion, notwithstanding the various measures which were adopted to facilitate or insure its success. On the late occasion, in the year 1833, the employment of the State banks was guarded especially in every way, I which experience and caution could suggest. Personal security was required for the safekeeping and prompt payment of the moneys to be received, and full returns of their condition were, from time to time, to be made by j the depositories. In the first stages the mea- j sure was eminently successful, notwithstanding the violent opposition of the Bank of the United States, and the unceasing efforts made to overthrow it. The selected banks performed with fidelity, and without any embarrassment to themselves or to the community, their engagements to the Government, and

the system promissed to be permanently useful. But when it became necessary, under the act of June, 183<>, to withdraw from them the public money, for the purpose of placing it in additional institutions, or of transferrin" into the States, they found it, in many cases, inconvenient to comply with the demands of the Treasury, and numerous and pressing applications were made for indulgence or relief. As the instalments under the deposite law became payable, their own embarrassments, and the necessity under which they lav of curtailing their discounts and calling in their debts, increased the general distress, and contributed, with other causes, to hasten the revulsion in which, at length, they, in common with the other banks, were fatally involved. Under these circumstances, it becomes our solemn duty to inquire whether there are not, in any connexion between the Government and banks of issue, evils of great magnitude, inherent in its very nature, and against which no precautions can effectually guard. Unforeseen in the organization of the Government, and forced on the Treasury by early necessities, the practice of employing banks was, in truth, from the beginning, more a measure of emergency than of sound policy. When we started into existence as a nation, in addition to the burdens of the new Government, we assumed all thejarge but honorable load of debt which was the price of our liberty, but we hesitated to weigh down the in- j fant industry of the country by resorting to

adequate taxation for the necessary revenue. The facilities of banks, in return for the privileges they acquired, were promptly offered, and perhaps too readily received, by an embarrassed L reusury. During the long con- i tinuance of a national debt, and the intervening difficulties of a foreign war, the connection was continued from motives of convenience ; but these causes have long since passed away. VVe have no emergencies that make banks necessary to aid the wants of the Treasury ; we have no load of national debt to provide for, and we have on actual deposite a large surplus. No public interest, I therefore, now requires the renewal of a con- I nection that circumstances have dissolved. Unfortunately too, the evils of the system are not limited to the banks. It stimulates a general rashness of enterprise, and aggravates the fluctuations of commerce and the currency. This result was strikingly exhibited during the operations of the late deposite system, and especially in the purchases of public lands. The order which ultimately directed the payment of gold and silver in such purchases, greatly checked, but could not altogether prevent the evil. Specie was indeed more difficult to be procured than the notes which the banks themselves create at pleasure ; but still, being obtained from them as a loan, and returned as a deposite, which they were again at liberty to use, it only passed round the circle with diminished speed. This operation could not have beeu performed, had the funds of the Government gone into the Treasury, to he regularly disbursed, and not into banks, to be loaned out for their own profit, while they were permitted to substitute for it a credit in account. In expressing these sentiments, I desire not to undervalue the benefits of a salutary credit to any brancli of enterprise. The credit bestowed on probity and industry is the just reward of merit, and an honorable incentive to further acquisition. None oppose it who love their country and understand its welfare. But when it is unduly encouraged þÿ when it is made to inflame the public mind with the temptations of sudden and unsubstantial wealth þÿ when it turns industry into paths

that lead sooner or later to disappointment and distress þÿ it becomes liable to censure, and needs correction. Abuses of credit and excesses in speculation will happen in spite of the most salutary laws; no government perhaps can altogether prevent them ; but surely every government can refrain from contributing the stimulus that calls them into life. Since, therefore, experience has shown, that to lend the public money to the local banks, is hazardous to the operations of the Government, at least of doubtf ul benefit to the institutions themselves, and productive ol disastrous derangement in the business and currency of the country is it the part of wisdom again to renew the connection ? They gave to Congress express powers to coin money, and to regulate the value thereof and of foreign coin ; they refused to give it power to establish corporations þÿ the agents, then as now, chiefly employed to create a paper currency ; they prohibited the States from making any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts ; and tiie first Congress directed, by positive law, that the revenue should be received in nothing but gold and silver. Public exigency at the outset of the Government without direct legislative authority, led to the use of banks as fiscal aids to the Treasury. In admitted deviation from the law, at tiie same period, and under the same exigency, the Secretary of the Treasury received notes in payment of duties. The sole ground on winch the practice, thus commenced was then, or has since, been justified, is the certain, im-

j mediate, and convenient exchange of such notes for specie. Government did indeed receive tiie inconvertible notes of State banks during tiie difficulties of war ; and the community submitted without a murmur to the unequal taxation and multiplied evils of which such a course was productive. With the war, this indulgence ceased, and the banks were obliged again to redeem their notes in gold and silver. The Treasury, in accordance with previous practice, continued to dispense with the currency required by the act of 1789, and took tiie notes of banks in full confidence of their being paid in specie <ut demand ; and Congress, guard against the slightest viola- to tion of this principle, have declared by law, that if notes arc paid in the transactions of the Government, it must be under such circumstances as to enable tiie holder to convert them into specie without depreciation ot delay. Of my own duties under the existing laws, when the banks suspended specie payment, I could not doubt. Directions were immediately given to prevent the reception into the Treasury of any thing but gold and silver or sion and publicity, as to prevent the possibili- | its equivalent; and every practicable arrangetv of any serious abuse on the part of the I ment was made to preserve the public faith, by similar or equivalent payment to the public creditors. The revenue from lands hud been for some time substantially so collected, under the order issued by the directions of my predecessor. Tiie c fleets of that order
jiad been jv salutary, and it forecast ill rg.

gard to the increasing insecurity of bank paper had become so apparent, that, even before the catastrophe, 1 had resolved not to interfere with its operation. Congress is now to decide whether the revenue shall continue to be so collected or not. Tlie receipts into ttie Treasury, of bank notes, not redeemed in specie on demand, will not, I presume be sanctioned. It would destroy, without the excuss of war or puplic distress, that equality of imports, and ideDlity of commcicial regulation, which lie at the foundation of our Confederacy, aud would offer to each State a direct temptation to increase foreign þÿtrade by depreciating the currency received for duties in its ports. Such a proceeding would also, in a graat degree, frustrate the policy, so highly cherished, of infusing nto our circulation a large proportion of the precious metals ; a policy, the wisdom of which none can doubt, though there may be different opinions as to the exteul to which it should be carried. Its results have been already too auspicious, and its success is too closely interwoven with the future prosperity of the country, to permit us fora moment to contemplate its abandonment. We have seen, under its influence, cur specie augmented beyond eighty millions; our Coinage increased so as to make that of gold amount between August, 1834, and December, 1836, (o leu millions of dollars : exceeding the whole coinage at the mint during the thir'y one previous years- The prospect of funher improv meat continued without

abatemeut, until the in,m»-it of the suspension of specie payments This policy has now indeed hee'- suddenlv checked, but is still far from being overthiown. Amidst all conflicting theories, one position is m de- j nmole.- the precious metals will invariably disapp, ar when there ce i9es to be a necessity for their use as a circulating medium It was in strict accordance with this truth, that whilst, in ihe mouth of May last, they were every where seen, and wre current for all ordinary purposes, they disappeared from circulation the moment the payment of spicie was refused by the banks, and the community tacitly agreed to di pense with its employmant. Their place was supplied by a currency exclusively paper, and, of in many cases, of tha worst description. Already are (he bank notes now in circulation greatly depreciated, and they flue tuate in value between one place and another ; thus diminishing and making uucertam the worth of properly and the price of labor, and failing to subserve, except at a heavy loss, the purposes of business. þÿ With each succeeding day the metallic currency decreases ; by some it is boarded in the natural fear, that, once parted with, it cannot be replaced : while by others it is deverted from its more legitimate uses, for Ihe sake of gain. Should CoDgress sanction (bis condition of things, by making irredeemable paper money receivable in payment of public ones, a temporary check to a wise and salutary policy will, in all probability, be converted into its absolute destruction.

A correspondent wishes ns to insert l)r. þÿFranklin s epitaph on himself, this we do, merely observing that it is much less original than it has generally been considered : The body of Benjamin Franklin, Printer, Like the cover of an old book, Its contents worn out, And stripl its lettering and gilding, of Lies here food for worms. Yet the work itself shall not be lost, For it shall, as he believes, appear once more, In a new And more beautiful edition, Corrected and amended By the Author, The following, which is taken from an old work, published a century and a half before the time of Franklin, probably suggested the idea of his epitaph ; The world's a book, writ by the eternal art Of great the author ; printed in man's heart ; 'Tis falsely printed, though divinely prun'd ; And all the errata will appear ut the enit. Ami again The world's a printing house ; our words are thoughts ; Our deeds are characters of several sizes ; Each soul's a compositor, of whose faults The Is cites are correctors heaven revises. Earth is the com 'ion press, from which being driven, We're gather'd sheet by sheet, and bound for heaven. New York Paper.

MaKE KNOWN : That whereas it has been communicated to me by the Royal Westindia Government, that the Royal Ordinance of 30th May 1828, regarding several points to be observed in the ceremony of baptism ; and which Ordinance, with modifications answering to the Locality of the Danish Islands, has been made valid for said Islands, by the Edict of 6th April 1831, is not stiictly adhered to, by all the Inhabitants belonging to the Lutheran and Danish Missionary congregations. I deem it expedient, further to impress a due obedience to the abovementioned Royal Ordinance that it may in future be a guidance to all concerned. The principal points are these : þÿ Sec. 1. That Children who are to be made members of either of the above congregations, shall be baptized, in either of the respective Churches, in the Islands of St. Croix and St. Thomas, within 8 Weeks after their birth, and in the Island of St Johns within 4 Months. Sec. 2. That baptism, as a holy rite ought to be performed by the Minister of the Gospel and in the house of God, provided proof has not been adduced, that the iite of the child, through illness, might be in danger of being carried to church, in which case, the baptism may be

performed at home ; and should such illness continue until the child attains the age mentioned in Section 1, it nevertheless becomes a duty to have it baptised at home. Sec. 3. That the private (or home) baptism, shall always be performed by either of the respective Ministers, unless that the life of the Infant should be in immediate danger, and that the services of the former can not be obtained, then and in that case, the baptism may be performed by a protestant Minister, one of th þÿ Brethren of the Moravian sect or congregation, or any other ordained person, a Schoolmaster, or a well informed Christian of proper age and moral conduct, consequently the baptism may be performed by the child's father, but no midwife or any other female is permitted to officiate, unless that the feeble state of the child, connected with other circumstances, may prevent the obtaining in due time, the assistance of a male, endowed with the abovementioned qualities to perforin the baptism. Sec. 4. Should the time ordained by Law, having expired, for the baptism of the child, the Minister is then bound to remind the father, and if an illegitimate child, the mother, to obey the mandate of the Law, and if those concerned, do not at the very first Sunday of service, after such warning, conform with their duty, such obliquity of conduct, must immediately becommunicated by the Minister, to the Royal Westindia Government of St. Croix and to the Royal Council in St. Thomas, who will strictly enjoin the concerned, to have the
r,l)i'd christened the following sundav of service, subject to a fine from 1 to .0 Ps. D W. C. on non performance, and subsequently a

EASTS! VSSTCSKMSR tepition of the same fine will be exacted, each time that the service in the church takes place, without the due performance of baptism. Sec 5. In cases where parents have had their child baptised at home it is notw ithstanding incumbent on them, within the time limited by Section 1, to have the said baptism solemnized in the church in the usual manner, subject, on its non performance, to all the penalties as above recited, unless it can be proved that illness prevented the accomplishment thereof, in which case the Minister may grant a delay of 4 weeks, and renew such grant on further adducent proofs, at 4 weeks each time. Sec. 6. That every baptism performed at home, shall, within 8 days after, be communicated to the respective Minister, or in his absence to one of the church Wardens, by the person having officiated in the baptism, subject to a fine on non-compliance, as heretofore mentioned. Sec. 7. Should a baptism at home having been resorted to, and performed, without any efficient grounds by any other than the respective Minister, the culpable persons are liable to a fine of from 2 to 10 Ps. D. W. G. Sec. 8. That in order to facilitate a due observance of the baptism of all children at the time limited by Law, all births, shall within 8 days after, be communicated to the respective Minister, or in his absence, to one of the Church- Wardens, which communication is incumbent on the father, and in his absence, or when it is an illegitimate child, on the mother, or those around her, superintending her

domestic affairs, which her state may prevent her managing personally, subject to a fine, on non-compliance, of from 1 to 5 Ps. as heretofore mentioned, which fine, will be exacted, every subsequent week, until the communication takes place. Sec. 9. Should the Parents, ere the child has been baptized, remove from the Parish where it has been born, it is incumbent on them, within the limited time as mentioned in section 8 and liable to the same penalties, to give notice of the birth of the child to the respective Minister of the Parish to which they have removed, or in his absence to one of the Churchwardens, which communication in consequence of such removal, a certificate thereof must be obtained, and transmittted to the Minister of the first mentioned Parish. The foregoing Rules as well as those in the Royal Ordinance and Edict as heretofore mentioned, the latter of which, in all its parts have made them applicable to the upcmancipated. þÿ All Owners, their Attomies or those having the superintendence of them, are strictly enjoined to conform to the respective Decrees liable to all the penalties as above recited, on their non-observance. In order that the Royal Government in St. Croix and the Royal Council in St. Thomas may be enabled to enforce a due obedience to the above mentioned Laws, it is incumbent on all Ministers of the Lutheran and Danish Missionary Congregations in all the Islands, quarterly to transmit to the said Authorities, a correct statement of all the births during

the quarter year, accompanied by a declaration, if timely notice has been given of such births þÿ if the children have been christened within the limited time, either at homo or in church, and whether the parties have conformed to the Letter of the Law or have deviated from the Rules as therein prescribed. This Placard to be recorded in the Tribunals of the Islands and with a translation

AT3t3 thereof inserted in the newspapers, and to he circulated throughout all the Estates, in order that those concerned, may conform themselves accordingly. From the Barbadian, October 14. On Thursday last we had a prodigious fall of water, the heaviest experienced for the year. For the first tirne this year the stream which runs over the Roebuck gully and Constitution ran in a rapid torrent. A waterspout was seen by many persons. It appeared to observers in Black- rock to be about the size of a sugar mill, at a great height, and travelling first from North to South, and back again þÿ where it discharged itself we cannot tell, but there was an immense rush of w ind along with it, probably a whirlwind, from the effects which we are told it had in tearing up trees, and doing other injury. The young Queen of Portugal, and the Duchess of Orleans, are in a way to give heirs to the Thrones of Portugal and France. A Roman Catholic Prince (Duke of Orleans, eldest son of Phillippe of France) having married a Lutheran Princess, may produce important changes in the religion of a country almost exclusively devoted to Popery. It may considerably accelerate the impulse already given to the exertions of Protestant teachers on the Continent.
Our Queen Victoria is the only Sovereign ever known of that name, except one who swayed a portion of the VV estern Roman EmþÿP e
