(From the New York Enquirer, October 28.) The Susquehanna. þÿ We extract from the Philadelphia and other papers all they contain in relation to this vessel, in whose fate the public at present feels so much interest. From the Philadelphia United States Gazette. THE SUSQUEHANNA. We regret that the latest intelligence received last evening, would seem to corroborate, at least in some degree, the first report ot the capture of the ship þÿ Mr Rowland, one of the regular pilots from our river, and who was on board the pilot boat Mary Ann, which first discovered the piracy, has arrived in the city. He states that when he first saw the Susquehanna, she was sailing in a north-eastern direction, her regular course, which she continued until the ship was entirely lost sight of At a subsequent period the pilots discovered a ship bearing in a south-western direction. Supposing her to be probably inward bound and requiring a pilot, made towards her until reaching as near as to be able to discover that she was the Susquehanna. Iler sails were at this time partially bent, and the course she was then sailing, irregular and zig zag, was evidently caused by disorder on board. Alongside of the ship was a black looking schooner, answering to the description already given. After making this discovery, the pilot boat changed her purpose of boarding the vessel, and made immediately for the Capes, leaving tlie ship and her suspicious companion pursuing a south-western course until lost sight of in the distance. On arriving, the intelligence was without delay com-

municated to Mr. Rodney at Lewes, who despatched tlie information as already detailed. This apparent confirmation of the appaling outrage, has greatly tended to dispel the hopes that we have been led to indulge in, tliat tire intelligence might turn out erroneous. As it is, and taken in connection with the other reports which we publish this morning, we dread that our worst fears may yet be confirmed. Scarce a doubt however can exist, but that the fiendish gang who, if the reports should be true, have thus outraged every sense of justice and humanity, will be overtaken. The pirate can hardly esc;q>e the hot pursuit which has been ere this commenced from so many different points. The Globe, of Wednesday, has the following gratifying paragraphs : " We learri that after the news of the capture of the Susquehanna reached this city, on the evening of tlie 21th instant, orders were forthwith despatched to the Revenue Cutters at Wilmington, Norfolk, and Pensacola, by the Secretary of the Treasury. " They were directed by Mr. Woodbury to spare neither exertions nor expense, in putting to sea immediately, with a sufficient crew and armament, to capture tire pirate, and rescue her prize. " 'l'hcy were requested not to desist from pursuit till they had, if possible, accomplished these objects, or heard of their being accomplished by others. " We understand, also that similar directions were sent to Pensacola by the Navy Uepartinent, -to the commander of that station, and of the VV est India squadron."

a>A»3r Tttstrawxasx: ma©itai®aw®8 Tiie Proposition to Annex Texas to the United States. þÿ The National Intelligencer furnishes us with extracts from the correspondence submitted to the House of Representatives in obedience to the call of J. Q. Adams. The papers consist of a long letter from Mr. Hunt, the Texian Envoy, the answer of Secretary Forsyth, and the replication of Mr. Hunt. The National Intelligencer says, "The object of the letter of the Minister of Texas is to propose a negotiation for the purpose of annexing that country to the United States, which is pressed upon the Secretary of State by such considerations as w ill be substantially comprehended by a perusal of the reply of the Secretary of State." To General Memucan Hunt, &c. The undersigned, Secretary of State of the United States, has had the honor to receive the note of his excellency General Hunt, Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of Texas, dated the 4th instant, proposing a negotiation for the purpose of annexing that country to the United States. That communication has been laid before the President, who has considered it with just sensibility. In giving to the undersigned instructions to present, in reply, a prompt and decisive indication of the course it has been deemed necessary to adopt, the President indulges the confident expectation that no unfriendly spirit towards the Government or the people of Texas will or can be imputed to tlie United States. Neither tire duties nor the settled policy of the United States permit them to enter into

an examination of the accuracy of the historical facts related by General Hunt, nor to allow them, if even admitted to be correct, to control the decision of the question presented by him. The United States were foremost in acknowledging the independence of Mexico, and Imve uniformly desired and endeavoured to cultivate relations of friendship with that Power. Having always, since tiie formation of the Government, been exempt from civil wars, they have learned the value of internal quiet, and have consequently been anxious yet passive spectators of the feuds with which their neighbor has been afflicted. Although, in the controversy between Texas and Mexico, circumstances have existed, and events have occurred, peculiarly calculated to enlist the sympathies of our People, the effort of the Government has been to look upon that dispute, also, with the same rigid impartiality with which it has regarded all other Mexican commotions. In determining with respect to the independence of other countries, the United States has never taken the question of right between the contending parties into consideration. They have deemed it a dictate of duty and of policy to decide upon the question as one of fact merely. This was the course pursued with regard to Mexico herself. It was adliered to when analogous events rendered it proper to investigate the question of Texian independence. That inquiry was made with due circumspection, and the result was not arrived at until its probable conse-

quences bad been accurately weighed. The possibility of a collision of interests arising, among other causes, from the alleged superior aptitude of the climate and soil of Texas for the growth of some of tiie staples of the United States, was not overlooked. A sense of duty and a reverence lor consistency, howev-

A'rjs. er, it was considered, left this government no alternative, and it therefore led the way in recognizing Texas. A hope was certainly entertained that this act, and the motives that conduced to it, even if no other considerations were to have weight, would point out to the Government of Texas the propriety not only of cherishing intimate and amicable relations with this country, but of abstaining from other connexions abroad wliieh might be detrimental to the United States. Apart from this, however, it was presumed that Government would enter upon the execution of the intentions intimated by its envoy extraordinary, with respect to connexions with Foreign Powers, with a full understanding of the just and liberal commercial stipulations existing between the United States and other nations. A pervading principle of those compacts is impartial treatment of the citizens, vessels, and productions of the parties in their respective territories. It was not to be believed that the commercial allies of the United States would swerve from their engagements, no apprehension was felt that the interests of the country would suffer from the arrangements which Texas tyiglit enter into with hint. The question of the annexation of a foreign independent Slate to the United Slates, has never before been presented to this Government. Since the adoption of their constitution, two large additions have been made to tlie domain originally claimed by the United States. In acquiring them this Government

was not actuated by a mere thirst for sway ovi r a broader space. Paramount interests of many members of the confederacy, and the permanent well-being of all, imperatively urged upon this Government the necessity of an extension of its jurisdiction over Louis iana and Florida. As peace however, was our clicrished policy, never to be deported from, unless honor should be perilled by adhering to it, we patiently endured for a time serious inconveniences and privations, and sought a transfer of those regions by negotiation, and not by conquest. I he issue of those negotiations was a conditional cession of these countries to the United States. Tiie circumstance, however, of their being colonial possessions of Prance and .Spain, and therefore dependent on the mcliopolitun Governments, renders those transactions materially different from that which would be presented by the question of the annexiition of Texas. The latter is a .State with an independent Government, acknowledged as such by the United States, and claiming a territory beyond, though bordering on the region ceded by Prance, in the Treaty of the 30th April, 1803. Whether the Constitution of the United .States contemplated the annexation of such a State, and if so, in what manner that object is to be c fli.ct. ed, arc questions, in the opinion of the President, it would be inexpedient, under existing circumstances, to agitate. .So long as Texas shall remain at war, while the United .States are at peace with her

adversary, the proposition of the Texian Minister Plenipotentiary necessarily involves the question of war with that adversary. The United States arc bound to Mexico by a treaty of amity and commerce, which will lie scrupulously observed on their part, so long as it can be reasonably hoped that Mexico will perforin her duties and respect our rights under it. The United States might justly be suspected of a disregard of the friendly purposes of the compact, if the overture of Gent-

ral Hunt, were to be tven reserved for future consideration, as this would imply a disposition on our part to espouse the quarrel of Texas with Mexico ; a disposition wholly at variance with the spirit of the treaty, with the uniform policy, and the obvious welfare of the United States. 7'he inducements mentioned by General Hunt for the United /States to annex 'Texas to their territory are duly appreciated, but, powerful and weighty as certainly they are, light when opposed in the scale of reason to treaty obligations, and respect for that integrity of character bv which the United /States have sought to distinguish themselves since the establishment of their right to claim a place in the great family of nations. It is presumed, however, that the motives by which Texas has been governed in making this overture, will have equal force it) impelling Iter to deserve, as an independent Power, the most liberal commercial relations with the United States. Such a disposition will be cheerfully met, in a corresponding spirit, by this government. If the answer which the undersigned has been directed to give to the proposition of General limit should unfortunately work such a change in the sentiments of that Government as to induce an attempt to extend commercial relations elsewhere upon terms prejudicial to the United /States, this Government will be consoled by the rectitude of its intentions, and a certainty that although the hazard of transient losses may be incurred by a rigid adherence to just principles, no lasting

prosperity can be secured when they are disregarded. 'The undersigned avails himself of the occasion to offer General II tint renewed assurances of his very distinguished consideration. St. Croix, VHRISTIANSTED, (MONDA Y) November 27, 1837. Tiie Second October Packet arrived just after our last publication þÿ London dates of 1 (5th October are received. The civil war in Portugal appears to be terminated. The two Marshals Saldanha and Terceira having been defeated by the Constitutional army, the ti oops of the former have joined the Constitutional forces; þÿ Saldanha fc Tereeira were expected in England the Queen of Portugal þÿ has resolutely refused to degrade the two Marshals the young Prince has heen chris- þÿ tened with great ceremony, he has received nearly twenty names, and has the title of Duke of Braganza ; the consort of the Queen is to have the title of King. Don Carlos continued his retreat to the mountains; Espartero, Oroa and Carondolet, all in pursuit þÿ a thousand Carlist prisoners had arrived in Madrid. In France all eyes are turned to the expedition against Constantino, which appears to be under the command of the Duke De Nemours, þÿ aitho' principally directed by General Damrcmont fears are entertained of the re- þÿ sult, as the Bey of Constantine is said to have 9,000 þÿCavalry in addition the city is garrisoned by 5,000 Turks; and innumerable bodies of Ivarbiles are spread over the country þÿ the expedition commenced its march from Bona the 1st of October. The French Chambers have been dissolved and a new election rs to be made in November þÿ the death of the Duchess of St Lou is announced ; she was the wife of Louis Bonaparte, ex King of Holland, and daughter of the Empress Josephine þÿ her decease is said to have heen

hastened by the unfortunate plot in which her son Louis Napoleon had engaged, she was born in 1783. Queen Victoria had made a triumphant entry into Brighton, where splendid illuminations and rejoicings took place þÿ great preparations were making in London for the dinner to be given by the city to the Queen on the 9th of November ; twenty four thousand Pounds Sterling had been voted to defray the expence.

The Home steamer lately wreckedatx.v.was about 700 tons burtlten, upwards of 200 feet in length, and cost nearly & 100,000 þÿ we understand Insurance to amount of $40,000 only had been effected upon her.

Bell's Weekly Messenger of October 16th, announces the death of the Queen of Holland at tlie Hague, Oct: 1 2thþÿ Her Majesty was born in 1774, aird she was a daughter of Frederick William the 2d, King of Prussia þÿ Her decease is deeply regretted in Holland.

A most superb review of Fifty Thousand Cavalry took place at Wosnescnk in Russia, in August last þÿ the Emperor commanded in person ; þÿ the Empress, the vouug Czar, and many foreign Noblemen were present, the effect was grand and imposing, þÿ it is said that never, before in modern times, lias so large a body of Cavalry been re-united, þÿ not even by Napoleon in bis famed expedition to Russia in 1N12.

Barbados Mercury, November 11. Our statement of produce shipped from the island in the present year, oilers much upon which we can congratulate the agricultural interest. In the first place we believe tiie crop is larger than for any year preceding þÿ at least for a very long period ; and next> that it exhibits something like a satisfactory working of the apprenticeship. It must not however be forgotten in the account, that a great deal of land which has been allotted to cane cultivation since 1834, was before then, planted in corn roots, &c þÿ an obvious cause of the increased quantity of sugar made and exported The seasons for the year, if we except a few weeks of hard weather, and the consequences of the recent high winds, have been also propitious to the planter, and if to these considerations, we add the favorable state of the British markets throughout the year for colonial produce, there is not much cause for very heavy complaint. That the field 'aborers have, in some cases, manifested an inclination to be idle, we believe will hardly be denied, but then these eases have been few þÿ we are happy to say very few, and taking the praedials as a body, both old and young, we may observe that their general conduct deserves commendation rather than reproach. Whether the same propitious state of affairs will continue after the period of apprenticeship, is latlier subject for specu" lation than otherwise, unless we instance the orderly, quiet, and contented demeanor of the field laborers in Antigua, who were from the

first exempted by their masters from the apprenticeship, and have since shewn a willingness to labor, which could have been hardly expected from a people not accustomed to regulate their own actions, and who were dependent in every sense of the word, upon their owners for the necessaries of life. Upon the whole we are however inclined to angur favorably of our island peasantry þÿ at least of the better classes of them; they will, like the Antigonians, see the necessity of working for their daily subsistence, and feeling this necessity, they will and must obey its impulse: there may be indeed some few of tliein, who will prefer a quite opposite course of life þÿ who will depend more upon the labors of others than their own exertions; but with wholesome laws to remedy the evil, there can be no very great room for serious apprehension upon this score. At any rate, we are not disposed to look at the gloomy side of coming events. In the interim, we can but hope that all things will work together for the good of all, and that we shall have it in our power, at the close of many a forthcoming year's crop, to place before our readers as gratifying a report as that which wc now submit. Review op the Troops .at Windsor by iieb Majesty. On Thursday afternoon (as we stated yesterday) the Queen reviewed the first regiment of life guards, under the command of Colonel the Hon. Henry Cavendish ; the 12th lancers, commanded by Colonel Barton ; and the 2d battalion of grenadier guards, under Colonel Joddrel!. The review took place in the Lower Park. Her Majesty, upon a grey charger, richly caparisoned, and dressed in the Windsor uniform, decorated with the star and order of tiie garter, arrived in the Home Park at three o clock, attended by the Piince Charles of Lichtcnetein, and Baron Ueisdach; Lord Hill, the general commanding-in-chief ; General Sir George Quintin, equerry of the crow n stables I the Marquis of Conyngham, the Lord Chamberlain ; Lord Torrington, the Lord in waiting ; Lord Alfred Paget, equerry in wailing; the Hon. Charles Murray, groom in waiting; and Master George Cavendish, page of honour, in their respective uniforms. Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Ktnt, and Miss Cavendish, her Majesty's maid of honour, were also mounted in the royal suite. After the royal salute her Majesty rode along the ranks and inspected the troops with great minuteness. They then passed her Majesty in parade honour ; the infantry in slow and quick time, and in column at quarter distance. The cavalry at a walk, trot, and gallop, left in front. The following movements were then performed : þÿ Infantry, Prom original line advanced in column from the right, and formed line to the front ; retired, formed square upon the cen-

tre ; formed line, and retired by files from the right of companies. Cavalry advanced by threes from the right of squadrons, and attacked. Inlautry, Column, at quarter distance. Cavalry, Retired in echellon from both flanks; fronted and retired in open column from both flanks. Infantry, Column advanced, formed square, and lircd. Cavalry, Formed close column of squadrons, right in front, took ground to the right, advanced, displayed in front of infantry, attacked by squadrons in succession, and formed line to the front ; lancers pursuing. Infantry, Re formed column, and deployed into line on a centre company. Cavalry, Retired in two lines, covered bv skirmishers ; formed line, retired in open column from the centre round the flanks of the infantry. Infantry advanced, covered by skirmishers. Cavalry, In double column. Infantry advanced, fired a volley and charg. cd ; retired in line ; halt, front, and opened centre companies.

Cavalry advanced in double column, formed line to the front, and charged, lancers pursuing. Infantry, Formed quarter distance column. Cavalry, Retired in open column from both flanks, and took up their original line. Infantry took up their original line.. Cavalry and infantry advanced in parade order. Royal salute. The bands playing " God save the Queen." Her Majesty was graciously pleased to express to the officers commanding the different corps, in the strongest terms her Majesty's high approbation of the appearance and discipline of the troops. Her Majesty left the ground at half past four, escorted by the lancers. Nothing could exceed her Majesty's graceful deportment on horseback, and the scene altogether was of the most gratifying description. A great many families of distinction were in the Park, and the North Terrace was completely crowded with þÿspectators. Morning Herald, September 30.

Well done, Brother Jonathan I þÿ »ooo TURK EY. CONSTANTINOPLE, July 19. A grand Council, presided over by the grand Vizier, was held on Saturday last at the Porte. As the question about to form the subject of debate was one of superlative importance not only the principal officers of the empire, but every Mussulman authority held in requte for wisdom, was summoned to attend the meeting. It was proposed first to the Assembly to inquire into the cause of the alarming deterioration the morals of Turkish females had within the last few years visibly undergone ; and secondly to point out the measures best calculated to arrest the progress of an evil which endangered the stability of the very basis of the Mussulman social edifice It was unanimously decided that the proximate cause of this growing looseness of

public morals was tiie emancipation to which females in general had arrived from the restraints imposed upon their liberty by the Alcoran and the customs and habits of the East, and consequently that it became the duty of the guardians of public virtue to tighten anew the fetters from which they had been imprudently suffered to exonerate themselves. A finnan to be read in every mosque in the capital was drawn up, under the dictation of the Grand Vizier, whereiu Mussulmans, after being severely rebuked for their remissness in watching over the proceedings in tbsir

harems, are enjoined to become in future more vigilant, strenuously to oppose themselves to its inmates leaving its precincts to appear in public without an urgent reason, and when under the necessity of granting this permission to insist on their being accompanied wherever they went by a trustworthy person. This firman not being considered sufficient to render the frailer portion of the sex proof against surrounding dangers it was resolved, the more efficaciously to secure their virtue, to remove the most alluring source of temptations þÿ the Christian youths who serve as apprentices in the shops of the capital. A second firman, to be read in every place of religious worship frequented by unbelievers, was issued, ordering Greek, Armenian, Catholic, and Jewish shopkeepers to dismiss from their employ every man below the age of thirty þÿ to oblige those above that age to lay aside the new dress, such as Mussalmaus wore, and to replace it with the black turban and bumble garb of Rajahs. þÿ The same mandate threatens them with the severest punishment in the event of their permitting Turkish females to enter their shops, or speaking to them on subjects foreign to their trade. The beneficial results of these wise regulations have already become apparent, and the streets of the city, once the resort of the Moslem beau monde, look now as desert and desolate as if the scythe of the plague had moved down the whole of this interesting portion of the population. These reforms have so much taken up pub-

lic attention that the arrival of General Cass> the American Ambassador at Paris, has hardly been noticed by Turks. The object of his visit to the Turkish capital has not yet been ascertained. Many are of opinion that it has no other but the gratification of a tourist's curiosity others, : that the General is entrusted with a special mission of great importance. The better informed among the Turks gravely affirm that, tired of democracy, the Americans have directed General Cass to soliei t " the distributor of the Crowns' to confer on their nation the favour of also placing one at its disposal. As by way of backshish, it is added several millions in gold have been placed on board the Constitution, the Turks are inclined to believe that the Sultan may ultimately be prevailed upon to comply with the General's entreaties, especially as at the present crisis the imperial cotters happen to be almost empty. þÿ London Weekly Post, August J 3.

Notice on Ai.ar.m Gono. þÿ A very ingenious instrument, of which we have seen a model, has been invented by Captain George , Smith, R. N., intended to give warning of the approach, and to announce the course a steamer is sailing on in a fog. It consists of a gong, on which a hammer is made to strike everv ten seconds a certain number of blows, by very simple machinery, according to the course a steamer is sailing on. For example, if she he sailing north, the gong is struck once ; if east, twice ; if south, thrice ; and if west, four times, every ten seconds. By this systematic method the position, course, and proximity of a steamer will be clearly announced to any other vessel. In rivers Captain Smith proposes the gong to emit single sounds every ten seconds, which would be enough to give warning. He also proposes to" apply the- instrument to railway trains, by tfie blowing, of a trumpet. The peculiar merit of tlie invention appears to us to lie in
the equability of intervals, and of intensity id sound, which cannot be equalled by any human means. þÿ Railway Magazine.

From the Greenock Advertiser, October 9. The French papers are chiefly occupied with the preparations making for the contemplated attack upon Constantina. Cholera however, had made its appearance among the French troops at Bona, which, it was thought, would delay the expedition till another season. At a council of war, held on the 24th ult., it was agreed that no attack should be made upon Constantina till the arrival of reinforcements from France, 'l ite force of the enemy is stated, as exceeding 40,000 men, and an intercepted letter from their camp asserts in the metaphorical language of the East, that in the opinion of the prophets and marabouts, as many Frenchmen would be needed in order to take Constantino as it would require of ants to remove an egg from within a pot of milk ! It would be somewhat difficult to ascertain the number of insects requisite for such exploit, and we suppose an the French general would be very little the wiser of the information furnished by the letter in question. The principle item of domestic news in the French papers relates to a new creation of peers upon a somewhat large scale. The Moniteur of Wednesday contains a list of no fewer than fifty persons who are at once to be sent to the Upper Chamber. The Sun, in recording this fact, says þÿ " The example of so extensive a creation of Peers might be safely and prudently followed by Lord Melbourne. We are sadly in want of a batch of some fifty or a hundred liberal peers, to neutralize the /Junoverian policy of the House

of Lord." The Spanish papers announce positively that the treaty of peace and amity between Spain and Mexico has been signed by the Queen Regent, by which she renounces all pretensions to the sovereignty of Mexico.

Raynal of the Merchants' Exchange, for the following detail of an attempt to capture the brig Margareth, Smith, 1 1 days from New York, arrived in our river. " Brig Margaret reports, that on the 2d instant, the Island of Cuba in sight, was chased all day by a piratical schooner, apparently a Spanish vessel ; with a crew of 70 or 80 men þÿ towards night, the schooner neared the brig, and ordered her to come to ; the order not being obeyed, the pivot long gun of the pirate was pointed and matches lit to fire into the Margaret ; in consequence of such preparations the brig hove to þÿ a boat was lowered from the schooner, and several men, armed with muskets, pistols, cutlasses, &c. put ofi to board the brig þÿ a heavy sea running and the wind blowing fresh, when about midway between the schooner and the brig, the boat sunk. The Margaret immediately made sail and stood ofT before the wind ; after some delay, the pirate again gave chase þÿ after running sometime saw a brig on the wind showing light, a and lost sight of the pirate the for night. Next morning saw the schooner at anchor off Tortugas bank ; she a third time made chase for the Margaret until night, when the Margreth, put out her lights, hauled close to the wind for hours, and then stood on her course þÿ in tire morning saw nothing of the pirate."

U. S. Ship Independence þÿ Emperor of Russia. Capt. Richardson, of þÿ brig Leonidas, from Croostadt, arrived at Boston, informs the Messrs. Topliff (who furnishes this intelligence,) that the United States ship Independence sailed from Cronstadt on the 13th of August. Being all ready for sea and the wind light, the Emperor directed a boat with an officer and boat's crew, to be sent from every Russian ship of war in the harbor, to assist in towing the frigate out ; and Captain Richardson says that she went out of the harbor in fine style, with a string of boats nearly half a mile long in advance. The Emperor's attention to the frigate and her officers were unremitted, to the last moment of her stay at Cronstadt ; and it was remarked that no ship of war, of any nation, had ever before been known to receive such manifestations of good will, in a Russian harbor.

Lock your Bedroom Doors ! þÿ The following whimsical affair occurred lately at Marseilles, where it appears to have afforded much matter for merriment : þÿ A worthy citizen, returning home rather late, went by mistake one floor higher than he ought to have done, and very innocently walked into a room where another citizen, no less worthy than himself, had quietly consigned himself to slumber by the side of his own liege and legitimate lady. The summer night was not too dark for our intruder to be able to find his way into bed without the aid of a candle, and accordingly he proceeded without more ado to disrobe himse'f. In the act of getting into bed his hand encountered the haii v head of his unconscious neighbor, and the horrid idea immediately suggested itself that the w ife ot his bosom had proved frail, and that another had leaped into his seat. Furiously he raised his fist and discharged blow after blow on the unoffending countenance of his supposed rival. It takes but little time to awake even the soundest sleeper under so effectual an application The beaten man started up, but his antagonist had the advantage ol him, and was not to be prevailed on for a moment to desist from the merciless discipline which he was in the act of inflicting. The screams of the frightened wife soon brought other inmates of the house to the field of battle, and then, at length, an eclaircissement ensued þÿ The choleric gentleman was now as angry with himself as he had before been with his

unoffending neighbor, though he does not appear to have inflicted an equally severe punishment upon his own stupid head as upon that of his fellow-lodger. On descending to his own room he found his wife fast asleep in his own bed. The poor neighbor overheard was the worst off of the whole party. He was soundly buffetted, and his swollen and disfigured face did not allow him for several days afterwards to venture abroad.

To me there seems nothing in the world more preposterous than the perpetually itching desire of so many people for what is called "society." What can they find in society to compensate for the vexations which ever attend upon ceremonious intercourse? Unless people be as low in the creation as mere monkeys, and take delight simply in the chatter and the mischief going on around

them, I do no', see what they are to find in ordinary society to give them satisfaction. þÿ What is there in " Evil tongues, Rash judgments, and the sneers of selfish men, The greetings where no kindness is, and all 'The dreary intercourse of daily life," to satisfy the mind and heart of any one who thinks and feels? Yet I appeal to all persons of experience whether the things enumerated by the poet in the above lines be not the staple commodities in that traffic of mankind which is called an intercourse of society Oh well may it be called " dreary." Solitude is often sad, but except to diseased minds it is not harsh sorrow, nor does it call up feelings of sorrow and vengeance þÿ of contempt and hatred ; but he who thinks, and feels, and yet can bear the malicious clack of evil tongues þÿ the rash, headlong, presumptuous opinions þÿ the " greetings where no kindness is" the hollow flippant hypocriscies of the þÿ crowd one meets and talks withal þÿ he who can hear all this, without having the harsher feelings aroused within him, must be possessed of some secret which 1 have as vet to discover.

The maestro was so touched with this neck breaking enthusiasm that he not only offered to give him instructions, but has actually taken him with him to America. þÿ Musical World.

Description of Bonaparte, by Mcrcier, in 1804. þÿ "Bonaparte is of the middle size, a little stooping, thin, of somewhat a delicate frame, and nervous ; his hair is of a deep chesnut, falling over a large forward ; his eyes are laige, dark, quick, arid piercing, aquiline nose, a raised ehin, like that of Apollo Belvedere, pale complexion, hollow cheeks, a voice unrestrained and composed ; he listens attentively to those who speak to him, and answers briefly ; his air is solemn, but open ; be has not the austerity which characterizes the head of Brutus ! you may judge from his address that he is a t( inperate meditative man, but tenacious in ti e point which he has in view ; that his pale countenance reddens in a decisive action : that his body is all nerve, like that of a lion ; that he fights in the same way ; that he is indefatigable and flies like lightning towards the enemy, before whom he never knew fear; this fire is concentrated, he reserves if for great and strong explosions, and it does not imprint on his motions that restlessness natural to men who are only ardent, and who have not the faculty of sel<-p©»session."

From the London Times, Sept. 15, 1837 ) CAPTAIN BACK. nom a young officer who accompanied cattain back in his late perilous voyage. (From the Standard) After having given vent to the outpourings ot his grateful feelings to the Almighty for his mere.v in again restoring him to his family and his friends, lie proceeds thus : þÿ " And now for some account of our expedition ; and an extraordinary one it has been þÿ unsuccessful, I am grieved to say, to tho very dregs ; but never. I believe, has any one before been so thwarted in all human attempts, exposed to such continual hardships and dangers, and yet been so providentially fortunate in escaping from them. YVe made a tolerably fair passage across the Atlantic, considering the then crowded state of the ship and the bad weather we experienced. þÿ On the 29th of July (having sailed on the 16th of June, 1836) we fell in with the first ice, meeting great many bergs, and an unusual a quantity of the former ; keeping on the north side of Hudson's Strait, we reached the Upper Savage Islands on the Gth of August, where we were visited by the Esquimaux, and succeeded in bartering many articles ; it was there, too, we overtook the Hudson Bay ship that had sailed ten days before us, but we could not succeed in communicating with her, as we were in the land-water, and they beset in the park ; this was a grievous disappointment to us all, the whole having written long letters the moment wc saw her. However, wc were obliged to bear with it, but hoped you would derive pleasure by their

reporting us so far advanced on our voyage. Wc made the Mill and Trinity Islands on the 1 5th of August, off whose rugged and barren shores we were detained beating three days, making little or no progress, from the strong current that set down from Fox's Channel ; a slant favoured us at last on the morning of the 18th of August, under whose influence we ran till the 20th( when we made the immense northern barrier of ice coming down Fox's Channel. From that date our troubles began, and, notwithstanding the greatest exertions on our part, we were unable to master them. It mattered not, at noon or midnight, fair weather or foul, whenever a lead or an opening in the ice presented itself, all hands, by our admirable and energetic commander, tremendous pressure of the sea-ice carried were set immediately to work þÿ boring the vessel under canvass through ice that threatened every moment to stave the ship, and at other times warping with our whole lives along immense floes, the temperature, even at that time, so cold that the boats were frequently obliged to break the bay ice as they went along to layout the warps, and the lines themselves were coated with ice as we hauled them in. By efforts like these we succeeded in crossing Fox's Channel, and on the 1st of September we were only 120 miles from Repulse Bay, but still beset in the ice ; at that time the least sanguine on board expected we should reach Repulse Bay, or at least some harbour, where we might have secured the ship for the winter : but Provi-

dence ordained it otherwise. September passed, during the latter part of which the ship was twice so severely nipped with ice, at one time hove up abaft seven feet six inches, that we feared her parting from under us, and we found ourselves still (and as it

3>AXT3X T33TCIITO331C 3383333XTG3 AT33. eventually turned out, fixed for the winter) in the open ice. YV e thus became the very children of circumstances, perfectly helpless as to the command of our ship, being completely at the mercy of the tides and winds. YVinter closed rapidly on us, and from our oxposed situation we were unable to make those arrangements for guarding against the cold that we should have done had we been in port Our warming apparatus, which you may recollect failed in almost the first attempt to use it, and all our endeavours to repair it, were unsuccessful, the pipes continually bursting. By using stoves and leading copper funnels along the lower deck we succeeded in raising the temperature to a considerable height below ; but then everything was literally steaming with wet þÿ bed clothes, books, and all our traps, and we were indeed in a dreadful state. In the beginning of November sickness laid its leaden hand upon us, and that horrid disease the scurvy broke out with great violence ; by the end of the year we had one third of the crew on the sick list, and more than two-thirds were more or less affected with it, and miserable and disheartening it was to the remainder, when dragging their sick shipmates over the ice for exercise, in sledges made of the staves of casks, to see their sallow countenances, their crooked and deformed legs, one principal feature of the disease. But, notwithstanding these misfortunes, we kept our hearts up, hoping that the spring would release us, and that, under tho

cheering influence of the sun, our sick would mend. YVe were driven with the wind and tides alternately to the Eastward and YVestward, along the shore of Southampton Island, occasionally approaching it so close that we were enabled to make a hasty trip on shore by walking over the ice. This, from our situation, was somewhat hazardous, but which few minded, as we would, I believe, have undertaken anything at that time to vary our existence. By the end of December the floepiece in which we were beset, and which at one lime was seven miles in circumfcience, began gradually to diminish from the pressure of the surrounding ice, and having in January been driven a long way to the S E. we found ourselves in the vicinity of excessively strong tides, or rather races, where the ice was running with great velocity ; bowever, our floe held on bravely until I the 17th of February, or rather the morning of the 18th, at 3 a. in. (my being on watch), when the

every thing before it ; our poor floe, that had befriended us so long, went with a surge; waves of ice, tanging from 20 to 30 feet high, absolutely running all round us, and the ship was at one moment in the water, and at another closely beset, suffering dreadful pressure ; from that day untill the end of March our existence was not only harassing, but dreadful in the extreme ; the ship was strained so severely that we were obliged to shore the upper and lower decks up witli spars, to cut up others to make additional athwart supports ; the upper deck was lashed down to the lower deck beams with lashings of a fiveinch hawser, the heavy strains on the topsides having caused it to rise up when under pressure to an extent that made us fear its bursting up altogether. I'rovisions and stores of all descriptions were got on deck, our boats hoisted halfway up the lower rigging to keep them clear of the ice ; every man had, by the captain's directions, his little bag, containing one change, slung all ready on deck and no man was permitted to undress when he lay

down to rest. Things went on in this state, the ship at one time risen up five or six feet by the ice, then heeling 10 and 12 degrees to starboard or poit, as may he, each succeeding day carrying us nearer and nearer to the land barrier, of which 1 am afraid 1 cannot give you a sufficient idea. It was the ice that had attached itself fo the shore during the winter, and its outer edge, varying from 20 to 60 feet in height, presented a perpendicular front smooth as glass, from the continual rubbing of the sea- ice along it YVe were in the latter, and each succeeding day brought us closer to this dreadful barrier, where, had we but once touched, no earthly power could have saved us. On the 11th of March we were thrown up five feet fore and aft by the immense pressure, heeling 12 degrees lo starboard, the ship at the same time beginning to make water. On the afternoon of the 14th of March we had approached within 300 or 400 yards of the land barrier, when the ice commenced running in a perfect race, and the ship was hove up nearly eight feet abaft, our outer stcrnpost (the rudder had been long unshipped) split in two from the 10 feet mark downwards, the vessel making at the same time three feet water an hour. This was at 3 p. m., and the moment the ice was quiet we lowered four of our boats, and hauled them to the apparently strongest floe pieces to seaward of us, and there placed a great quantity of provisions and fuel by them, expecting, should additional pressure take place, our

near vicinity to the land harrier would cause the total destruction of the ship. The ice was then quiet until 10 p. m., when, with :t tremeridons roar, it became suddenly in motion, and an enormous barrier 20 feet in height, and resembling the crest of a heavy surf when about lo break, began rapidly to mow down the floe piece on which two of our boats were placed, and in a few minutes they must have been ingulfed by it. The hands were turned up, every man that had strength to drag his legs after him hurled himself over the ship's side, rushed along the loose and running ice to save the boats, for we knew, should the ship be crushed, our only chance of existence and reaching England was in saving them. Never shall 1 to the latest hour of my life forget that horrid night: it was blowing neatly a gale of wind, with a piercing snowdrift, and the tempcratuie was 40 degrees below the freezing point, the ice breaking and running from under our feet, so that we could scarcely keep our footing for one minute, and the awful sight of the wave of ice approaching us rapidly with a roar that made it impossible to hear a word spoken made us strain every nerve vvc possessed with such ctlect that we succeeded in saving our two bouts anil almost all our provisions ; but at 50 minutes past 12 the ice commenced setting in a succession of rushes against the ship's stern, causing her to make such an additional quantity of water, that we were obliged to man all four of the pumps, when a terrific rush of a

wave of ice 30 feet high, having on its top an enormous piece of solid ice, swept athwart our stern : two other barriers of ice look us one on each quarter, and their united eftorts seemed as if at length tliev wanted either to crush or overturn the ship, the latter all the time trembling and complaining most dreadfully, the lower deek beams rising, the planks starting, and at that moment there were lew, if any, but who cxj>ectcd a few minutes would

bring them into the presence of their Maker. Hut Cor! was merciful I the ship rose over everything, absolutely running on the top of two separate pieces of ice, the pressure of the ice at the same time stopping the leaks, so that one pump only kept her clear. By 3 the ice was quiet ; double allowance of meat was then served out to the ship's company, and all hands having been up for the last three nights, we lay down to rest, in the full expectation of having to desert the ship at the morning's dawn. At daylight we found ourselves literally on the top of the iec, the forefoot resting on the floe, and the ice was on a level with our tafl'rail. The ship was just before, or rather among one of the tremendous barriers of icc I have spoken of so much, the round of our fore-foot was ground down to the butt ends, and from the main channels six feet forward our side was indented to that extent as to make it highly probable that several of the timbers had given way. A council was held by the eap'.ain and the officers, when it was determined to leave the ship; but then everything was got on deck, ready for any emergency. Fifty sledges were made for dragging our provisions over the ice» should the ship part. Happily these precautions Were not required, as we remained perfectly secure in our elevated situation ; for, although the pressure was frequently afterwards as heavy on the surrounding ice as we had ever seen it, yet the barriers of ice by which we were surrounded seemed to pre-

serve us from any additional pressure. Well, we drifted down on the top of the ice till we arrived off" the Sea Horse point of Baffin, when a breeze at last came off the land, and we were set out into Fox's Channel, and eventually drifted down in the main body of the ice till wc arrived near Charles's Island, in Hudson's Strait. April and May passed, and as the sun seemed to have no effect on the ice, it was determined to attempt cutting the ship out : and this, incredible as it may appear, was finally. by the personal exertions of the officers and ship's company, accomplished. We had in the first instance to level from 14 to 20 feet in height of solid icc ; we began our work in the beginning of June, commencing at 5 p. m. Desperate hard work it was, but it was no trifle wc were woiking for þÿ the liberation of our ships and the return to our family and homes were objects to be accomplished, and for which wo would have worked till life was extinct. On the 3d of July wc commenced sawing through ice varying from 20 to 32 feet at the thickest, and from 14 to 20 feet at the thinnest. To effect this, we were obliged to weld two 20 feet ice saws together, and work them with ropes and sheers. On the 1 1th of July we had approached within a few feet of the ship's stern, when a sudden disruption of the ice took place, and the ship settled down, and at the moment wc thought she was free. The men, although many of them at the time were most perilously situated, being adrift on detached pieces of

icc, expressed their thanks by tremendous cheers. It was of short duration ; an immense piece of the floe remained attached to the ship, on our starboard side, auditor keel was completely imbedded in it. Every effort was made to shake it off', by making sail, and by sallying over from side to side ; and so, but without effect, we bad to commence sawing again Iroin the water's edge right into the ship's beam ; and having, by noon on the 13th, got within 12 yards of the ship, refixed the anchors on each side of the brack, and with double purchases of a six-inch hawser, bringing one across at the capstan and the

3&AW33R TasmsmstR other forward to the windlass, commenced heaving on the purchases, when the ice broke with u sudden crash, breaking off only the outer portion, the remainder, to the extent of eight yards front the ship, and on which the ship rested still being fixed to her bottom. þÿ This, from losing its counterbalance, and from its great buoyancy, threw the ship in a moment on her beam ends, Luckily the water was quite smooth with little wind ; all sail was reduced as quickly as possible, and the sea-boats cut adrift ; the ship then righted to Iter channels, but keeping 27 degrees to port, and making seven feet water an hour, kept the pumps going, as you may suppose, and got a large stage over the weather side, and the big saw under weigh, sawing the ice fore and alt close to the ship's side, every soul working there and at the pumps-- the batches battened down, and the boats stored with provisions and armed, in case of the worst þÿ continued working all that day and night þÿ serving out grog and solid meat occasionally. At 3 a. m , on July 14, having sawed twothirds of the ice, the captain ordered all hands in for two hours' sleep, all being quite exhausted. Scarcely were they below, when the ice parted suddenly, and the ship righted with a surge, when the wearied crew rushed on deck, and greeted the ship's descent into the water with loud and continued cheers. þÿ In fact, our feelings at the instant were too much for the whole of us. We had been 11 months beset in the ice þÿ 118 days literally on

the top of it ; but at last, through God's mercy, once more in our native element; and on the 8th of August we were in the open sea. clear of the ice ; and, though in a leaky ship that required all our endeavours to keep her free, yet all felt lightly the then difficulties we hud to look forward to."

FRANCE. Constantine is at length in the hands of the French þÿ t he following telegraphic dispatch conveyed the news to þÿl aris on the 23d inst. Lieutenant General Vallee to the minister of War. Constantine, Oct. 13. þÿ The tri-colored flag floats on the walls of Constantine, The army arrived before the walls on the 0th þÿ the breach was opened on the 11th þÿ was practicable on the I2th þÿ and this morning the assault was made with great bravery, and complete success
Our troops have triumphed gloriously. H. M. the King of the French and the ai my, have suffered a great loss was killed yesterday by a ball as he was ad-

inform you that I have succeeded him in the command of the þÿarmy. Prior to the assault both Generals addressed their armies on the eve of the onslaught as follows : Soldiers þÿ þÿ The expedition against Constantine is now under the walls of that city þÿ The Turks defended every house, and upon you devolves the honorable task of avenging your brothers in arms, who, betrayed by the elements, beheld last year, the failure of their courageous efforts under the walls of that city. The ardour and confidence which animate you forebode the success which awaits you. France has her eyes fixed upon you þÿ her fervent wishes and solicitude accompany you. Prove yourselves worthy of her, of the King who has confided to you one of his Sons þÿ of the Prince who has come to share your labors, and the country will glory in numbering you among its þÿchildren. Damremont. The following is Achrnet Bey of Constanþÿtine appeal s to his countrymen : þÿ The French have occupied Bona now three years, and we have tolerated them. þÿ They have þÿ appointed a Bey, the Unfaithful Joussouf, who called himself a Mussulman ; and who, whilst he commanded, committed all sorts of horrors. He bathed himself in the blood of his countrymen. Cut off their heads, and robbed them of every thing they possessed, for the purpose no doubt of enriching the French, since they winked at the sanguinary acts. The enemy of God came last to Stah el-Mansoura to þÿruin, to sack our noble city. I forced him to retire as you know.

Some days the French wished to make peace with us. I was as anxious for it as they were þÿ for the welfare of all ; but the conditions they required, were too onerous, too afflicting for true believers to be acceptable, as you shall see. They asked to be allowed to place a garrison of 3 or 4,000 men in the Casbah, to erect a fort at Stah-el-Mcssourah, and another at Condiat-ati þÿ they insisted on my paying them the tribute 1 paid the Dcy of Algiers þÿ together with seven years arrears due since they occupied country, the and finally upon my delivering up to them five hundred young virgins at their choice ! Children! will you accept these conditions at which I shudder and feel indignant ? If so, I shall mount my

A full supply of Jamaica and other colonial papers came to hand yesterday, brought by the steamer Carron, Lieut. Uwen. The new session of the Colonial Parliament was opened on the 21th ultimo by Sir Lionel Smith. þÿ The speech of his Excellency the Governor, delivered upon the occasion to the other two branches of the Legislature, is in another column, with the address of the Assembly and Sir Lionel's reply thereto. A long debate took place in the house on the 2t)th, on a motion being made by a member, Mr Leslie, to put an end to the apprentice-ships on the 1st of next August. Two amendments wore proposed to the effect that the question he open to the consideration of the house, on the basis of a fair, full, and equitable compensation by the British govern-

Mr. Leslie's motion was carried seventeen against eleven. þÿ It is with unfeigned pleasure (observes the Courant) we acquaint our readers that the tendered resignation of his Excellency Sir Lionel Smith, has not been accepted by her Majesty's government." After congratulating the inhabitants of Jamaica upon this fortunate event, the Courant indulges in the confident expectation that Sir Lionel will continue to maintain the high character he has established for justice and impartiality in public affairs, since his assumption of the administration of the government, The people of Jamaica, we know from experience, are fortunate indeed in their having to preside who um-.v iverns that highly flourishing and over the n f upright, conscientious individual prosperous colony ; they may be satisfied that the British government has consulted their best interests bv the rejection of Sir Lionel's resignation, and that the longer he remains with them the bettor it will be for all classes of the people. The new steamer Sir Lionel Smith had made her first trip round the island, greatly to the satisfaction of all on board. The accommodations are said to be excellent, although on a smaller scale than those of the City of Kingston. Two other company steamers, the Pearl and William IV., are expected in four or five weeks. DESTRUCTION OF THE COLONIST BY FIRE. ( From the Morning Ilerald, October 30 ) On Saturday the sad intelligence reached London ot oe almost total loss by fire, of the hu ge ship Colonist, a West Indiaman, at the Mother-bank þÿoil Portsmouth. This fine vesel left the London-doek, on Wednesday, with a valuable cargo, principally consisting of plantation stores, on a voyage to Barbados, and reached Portsmouth on the following evening, where she anchored tor the night. On the following morning, shortly before eight þÿo clock, the crew were engaged aloft miking preparations for getting the ship under weigh, when smoke was observed to issue from the hold up the main hatchway, and while hands were about to adopt active measures lor the suppression of the flames, the fire broke forth simultaneously from all the hatchways, and spread with the greatest rapidity. The passengers and people below were instantly aroused, and the terror and confusion on board was dreadful. The boats were directly lowered and the crew and passengers got into them. Many of the latter escaped in a state of almost complete nudity. The escape of one lady and her three children, who remained in the cabin until they were unable to ascend, was most miraculous. The mate observing their perilous situation, was lowered with a rope fastened round his waist, and he brought up the lady and her family, besides saving her cash and jewel-box, and other property of great value. In a few minutes the vessel was on lire from stem to stem, and the (limes ascended up the masts

forming a grand but awful sight. She continued burning until 10 þÿo clock yesterday m niiing. At that time the remains of the Colonist were towed ashore on the beach at Blockhouse Point, and when the last coach left Portsmouth at noon yesterday, the flames were not subdued. The Colonist was copper bottomed, and that alone kept Iter together for so many hours No part of Iter cargo was saved, and the whole interior of the vessel is destroyed, and a small portion other hull

The value of die vessel and her cargo has been variously estimated but is believed that the total loss cannot be less than 60,000/ Captain Smith the commander of tiie Colonist in his letter to the owners detailing the particulars of the calamity, states that the fire burst forth so suddenly that it was impossible to preserve anything, and that the crew and passengers were saved with much difficulty. He also says that he is þÿ indebted to the master of the Simon Taylor for the clothes he is standing upright þÿin. It appears that he was the last to leave the ship ; and that to his coolness and courage the passengers and crew are indebted for their lives. He is a great sullerer, having lost everything he possessed on hoard þÿ boet efter There were six mules, and a great many i sheep on deck, which perished in the flames ; one lady has lost a jewel-box, the contents of which are valued at upwards of 200/ ; a gentleman passenger has lost a gold watch and forty sovereigns derable loosers. Marionettes. þÿ Signor Bragaldi, advanta geously known as scene painter a and to the Italian opera, has been on visit artist to Italy, and has brought with him a new species of entertainment called Marionettes, which in some respects resemble w hat is known here as Fanlocini, only on a large and magnificent scale. þÿ It is a theatre, where the actors ate figures of about two feet and a half in height, and who go through entire plays, tragedy, comedy, opera and ballet, by machinery, aided by actors and singers w ho are unseen by the audience. This company consists of more than one hundred figures, modelled in composition, and exquisitely finished, with a wardrobe of 300 dresses of t lie most rich and splendid character, embracing every variety of character together with scenery, machinery, and properties, such as arc not to be found so full and complete in any theatre in this country. 'I he inventor of this new species of amusement is one Signor Girolino Garandara, of Milan, who had retired with a fortune, and it is a remarkable fact, that while the Last Days of Pompeii was produced at La Scala on a prodigiously magnificent scale, the same piece was played to crowded houses on the same night at the Teatro de Marionettes. It is said their ballet is wonderful þÿ they play La Bayadere, Sylphide, and all the great bullets, with the original ntusie, to the life, and th : figures make their pirouettes full as gracelully as Taglioni. þÿ N. Y. Star.

The correspondence which appeared in our last paper between Sir Henry Hardinge and Mr. Rowland Alston, proved this fact, that Sir Robert Peel had given instructions to Sir Henry Hardinge to call out, in his (Sir Robert's) name, Capt Townshend, had the latter not given Sir Henry complete satisfaction for the insult which Sir Robert Peel conceived he had received from him We frankly admit that, according to the principles of the world. Sir Robert Peel acted on this occasion with his accustomed spirit not without full provocation given, and, of course, proceeding under the advice of Sir Henry Hardinge, that crack master of ceremonies in these affairs of blood, with every punctilio, and in the exercise of all the proprieties which the occasion required ; and we cannot but rejoice that the affair ended with the offending party making a suitable apology to him who had been aggrieved, and this without the effusion of human blood, and the laws of the country being pubhekly outraged by one of the most distinguished of those who are peculiarly bound to do them honour. It is not, however, to be forgotten that Sir Robert Peel professes to be a religious man ; that in this, as in other respects, he is held up as a pattern to the country ; and especially, that the inaugural speech which he delivered upon his election to the office of Lord Rector of the University of Glasgow, was proclaimed throughout the kingdom to be a pure transcript off'hristian principle,

deserving a place in the library and in the heart of every intelligent youth in the kingdom. Many of our readers may remember that from this general decision we strenously dissented. We considered it our dntv to proclaim that the religious principles which Sir Robert Peel then endeavoured to press home upon the minds of his youthful auditory, were not the true principles of the Christian faith ; and we now, with equal, but not greater confidence, pronounce, that his practbc on this recent .occasion is equally opposed to the precepts of the Gospel. The principles he formerly disseminated were in reality the principles of the world, with merely a thin religious veil cast over them. The practice developed on this occasion is the practice of the world, without a veil, as it stands in direct opposition to the practice enforced by Jesus Christ. The principles naturally produced the practice. The tree has borne fruit according to its own nature, and that nature is not heavenly, but worldly Let us consider for a moment the system of duelling to which Sir Robert Peel, on other occasions beside this, has shown all readiness to be subject. It is a system which no one will have the hardihood to say, has its foundation in Christianity. It is a system to which those in the general pay the most scrupulous observance, who most notoriously trample under foot the laws of heaven. The defence of it is resolved into a matter of convenience or expediency : þÿ it is alleged to be useful in preserving deco-

rum and good manners among the higher circles of society, which could not be so well maintained by any other expedient. Hence it keeps its ground. And we have seen it-behests complied with by the most distinguished men oj the world whom the age has produced. Its laws arc well understood. If one gentleman receives what he considers an insult of a certain kind from another, instead of the difference being rclerred to any legal tribunal

Such a mode of settling a dispute is in entire and outrageous opposition to the whole spirit, and to every precept of the revelation of Jesus Christ. How is it possible, then, if Sir Robert Peel be a true Christian þÿ that is, an honest follower of Jesus Christ, carefully attempting to imbibe his spirit and obey his commandments þÿ he can be a duellist? We shall be happy to be furnished with any other satisfactory answer to the inquiry than that which we now offer, but till that is furnished, we give as a reply, that on this occasion his principles as a Christian, are lost in his principles as a man of the world, and that lie sacrifices Ins allegiance to Christ at the shrine of an absurd, unequal, cruel, and wicked practice of the world We repeat it, that in this matter the whole spirit and the direct commandment of Christ, is in diametrical opposition to the practice of the world. While, then, according to the laws of honour, we may not insult a fellowmortal, is it seriously thought that we may insult God with impunity ? That we may

profess ourselves the followers of our Saviour, and even commend his service to others, and turn round, and trample his precepts under our leet ? We may do it indeed ; but every man w ho so acts, sacrifices his duty to God to the foolish laws of a beggarly world, and assuredly, if be repent not, will eventually experience the awful truth contained in that test, þÿ ' God is not mocked."

as the Duke of Wellington and Sir Robert Peel, are without excuse in suffering this antichristian and shameful system so long to prevail. If either of them were to turn his | attention to find a substitute, and were he to recommend it, when found, to the Legislature with the zeal and earnestness which both exhibit in other matters of a mere worldly description, we are satisfied it would soon cease to exist. But w hat is it ? Only the command of God that is outraged ! Only the spirit and precept which our Saviour recommends which arc set at nought ! And age rolls on after age, and amongst a nation of professing Christians there stands the practice, a burning disgrace to them, arid a daring outrage on heaven It seems as if the nation were ambitious of writing the name of Hypocrite on its forehead.

The reis eflondi, or minister for foreign affairs, had a grandchild whose indisposition caused him the most lively uneasiness, it was in vain that his English physician assured him of the total absence of danger ; his every thought, every anxiety, were with his dar- his ling boy, in the midst of the most pressing public business, be would start up and hasten to the chamber of the little patient, to assure himself that every thing was going on favourairly ; he would leave his friends, in an hour of relaxation, to sit beside the sick bed of the child, and at length, when a strict and rigid system of diet was prescribed, which was to be of a fortnight's duration, he actually submitted himself, and compelled all his establishment to submit ; to the same monotonous and scanty fare, lest the bov should accidently see, or otherwise become conscious of the presence of any more enticing food, for w inch he might pine, and thus increase his malady. It may be thought that I have cited an extreme instance ; but such is, in reality, far from being the case, indeed, to such a pitch do the Osmnnits carry their love for children, that tltcy are constantly adopting those of others, whom they emphatically denominate

« children of the soul." They generally take them into their families when mere infants . they rear them with the most extreme care and tenderness ; and finally portion them on their marriage as though the claim were a natural, rather than a gratuious one. The adopted child of Turkey is not like the protege of Europe, the plaything of a season, and ultimately too often tlte victim of a whim: the act of adoption is with the Turks a solemn obligation ; and poverty and privation would alike fail to weary them of well doing, where their affections as well as their word were pledged An equally beautiful feature in the character of the Turks is their reverence and respect for the author of their being. Their wives advise and reprimand unheeded, þÿ their words are bosh þÿ nothing but the mother is an oracle ; she is consulted, confided in, listened to with respect and deference, honoured to her latest hour, and remembered with affection and regret beyond the grave. " My wives die, and I can replace them," says the Osmanli ; "my children perish, and others mav be born to me þÿ but who shall restore to me the mother who lias passed away, and who is no more ?" These are strong traits þÿ meuts, of human nature, and, it such be indeed the social attributes of barbarism," " then may civilized Europe, amid her pride of sciences and her superiority ol knowledge, confess that herein at least she is mated by the less highly gifted Mussulmans. The philosophy and kindly feeling of the

Turk is carried even beyond the grave. He looks upon death calmly and without repugnance : he does not connect it with ideas of gloom and horror, as we are too prone to do in Europe ; he spreads his burial-places in the sunniest spots þÿ on the crests of the laughing hills, where they are bathed in the light of the blue þÿsky besides the crowded thoroughfares of the city, where the dead are, as it were, once mingled with the living þÿ in the green nooks that stretch down to the Bosphorus wherein more selfish spirits would have erected a villa, or have 'planted vineyard. a He identifies himself with the generation which has passed away þÿ lie is ready to \ ield his place to that which is to succeed his own. Nor must 1 omit to remark on the devout and unaffected religious feeling that exists in Turkey, not only among the Mussulmans, however imperative may be their avocations, never neglect to pray five times during the day ; but equally among the Greeks and Armenians, whose fasts are so severe, that those of the Roman catholics are comparatively feasts. If you meet a Turk and enquire alter his health, he replies " Shukiur Allah! þÿ Praise be to God, I ain well." Every thing is referred to the Great First Cause. There is nothing of that haughty self-dependence, that over-wcening morgue , so strongly marked in Europeans. Among men, the Osmanli considers himself the first þÿ but only among men. When he puts off his slippers at the door of the mosque, lie carries no pomp with

him into the presence of his God. The luxuriant inhabitants of the East, who in his own salemliek is wont to recline on cushions, and to be served by officious slaves, docs not pass into the house of God to tenant a crimsonlined and well-wadded pew, and to listen fto the words of inspiration beside a comfortable stove, in dreamy indifference ; he takes his place among the crowd þÿ the effendi stands beside the þÿwater-carrier the bey near the

That the generality of the Turks hold every Frank in supreme contempt, admits of no doubt and could they, to use their own phrase, " make our fathers and mothers eat dirt," I am afraid that our respectable ancestors would never again enjoy a comfortable meal but this feeling on their part is rather amusing than offensive, and only enhances the merit of their politeness when they show courtesy to the stranger and the Giaout. If, as we are all prone to believe, freedom be happiness, then are the Turkish women the happiest, for they are certainly the freest individuals in the empire. It is the fashion in Europe to pity the women of the East; but it is ignorance of their real position alone which can engender so misplaced an exhibition of sentiment, I have already stated that they are permitted to expostulate, to ui ge» even to insist on, any point wherein they may feel an interest ; nor does an Osmanli husband ever resent. Part and parcel of his philosophy is to bear the stoim of words unmovbeautiful develop- I ed ; and the most emphatic and passionate oration of the inmates of his harem seldom produces more we shall see " It is also a fact, that though a Turk has undoubted right to enter the apartments of bis wives at all hours, it is a privilege of which

lie very rarely, may I almost say never, avails himself. One room in the harem is appropriated the to master of the house, and therein he awaits the appearance of the individual with whom he wishes to converse, and who is summoued to his presence by a slave. Should lie, on passing to his apartment, see slippers at the foot of the stairs, he cannot, under any pretence intrude himself in the harem ; it is a liberty that every woman in the empire would resent. When guests are on a visit of some days, he sends a slave forward to announce his approach and thus give them time and opportunity to withdraw. A Turkish woman consults no pleasure save her own when she wishes to walk or drive, or even to pass a short time with a friend ; she adjusts Iter y is h mac and Jeri/he, summons her slave, who prepares her boksha , or bundle, neatly arranged in a muslin handkerchief ; and. on the entrance of the husband, his enquiries are answered by the intelligence that the Hanoum Eflendi is gone to spend a week at the harem of so and so. Should he be suspicious of the fact, lie takes steps to ascertain that she is really there ; but the idea of controlling her in the fancy, or of making it subject of reproach on her return, is perfectly out of the question. The instances are rare in which a Turk, save among the higher ranks, becomes the husband of two wives. He usually married a woman of his own rank þÿ after which, should be either from whim, or family reason, resolve on increasing his establishment, he

purchases slaves from Circassia and Georgia, who are termed odaliques ; and who however they may succeed in superseding the Buyuk llatioum, or head of the harem, in his affections, are, nevertheless, subordinate per" sons in the household þÿ bound to obey her bidding, to pay her the greatest respect, and to look up to her as a superior. The almost total absence of education among Turkish women, and the consequently limited range of their ideas, is nnother cause of that quiet careless, indolent happiness that they enjoy their sensibilities have never are awakened and their feelings and habits been ever comparatively unoxactirig tliev have no facetious wants growing out ol excessive mental refinement ; and tlicy do not, therefore, torment themselves with the myriad anxieties and doubts, and chimeras, which darken and depress the spirit of some moie highly gifted females. St. James's Palace, Del. 11. þÿ The Queen has been pleased to appoint the Earl of Uxbridge one of the Lords in Waiting to her At ajesty. The Queen's Visit to the City. þÿ The intention her Majesty has expressed of proceeding to the city on the 0th of November next has caused a little bustle and excitement on the route it is expected her Majesty will take, and many are the plans in agitation aioong her Majesty's liege subjects as to the best tnode of welcoming their Sovereign on the occasion of her first visit to her capital, Tbe inhabitants of the Strand and other portions of the royal parish of St. Martin's- in the- Fields through which the procession will pass are concerting some plan of operations in order to signalise their loyally to our youthful Sovereign. By some it is proposed to erect a grand triumphal arch with flowers, banners, and emblematical devices, which, with the addition of a military band, would no doul-l have an imposing eflect. Others suggest having a grand grotesque pageant, after the fashion of the Shakspeare jubilee, with illuminations at night. The Strand will, it is expected, be gravelled all the way from Charingcross to Temple bar, and thecoiy d'ceil of the royal calvacade will no doubt be magnificent in the extreme. The poor t»f St. Martin's inthe-Fields, as well as of most of the city parishes, will it is expected, be regaled with old English fare þÿ roast beef and plum pudding, and everything is to wear the aspect of joyous mirth and hilarity. A contract has

been entered into with a house on I.udgatehill to illuminate Temple-bar on both sides and the exterior of Guildhall, so as to render these ancient fabrics one mass of Lamps, tastefully arranged for 450/. The lllue coat boys will be disposed in St. I'auls Churchyard, which no doubt will he an excellent point to view the cortege pass. The upholsterer's contract for lilting up Guildhall, the throne, and other decorations for the occasion, alone amounts

to 8000/. The work is now proceeding with the greatest celerity possible, and it is expected that the present will be the most magnificent display of civic pomp, wealth, and power, ever attempted in modern times. The tailors, milliners, and mantua makers are alreadv in full employ, and are putting forth circulars and advertisements, calling the public attention to the occasion ; and notices of first and second floors being to let to view the procession 011 tire line of road are quite common, and for which enormous prices are demanded. þÿ London Standard, Oct. 14.

The Tories have their troubles and uncertainties There is a most unwelcome suspicion among the more stanch and bigoted members of the party, that the Duke of Wellington may give as much assistance to Lord Melbourne as will enable him to carry the measures to which he is pledged, with some modifications. Others again care little what measures pass ; but to lend support without pay, to sit on the Opposition benches and vote with the Minister þÿ is what they cannot endure. Yet what is to be done ? The Court is with Lord Melbourne, and all the Tories who wish to be on good terms at C"iirt will find a reason for dividing with Ministers. This would be the commencement of a schism in the Tory ranks, and a consequent increase of strength to the Whigs, sufficient perhaps to keep their faction uppermost for a number of years. Thus we see that if the Whigs are embarrassed, the Tories arc perplexed. þÿ lb.

A Nmv Coach. þÿ There is now in course of building at a coachmaker's in the metropolis a coach of a description at onco novel, elegant, and safe. It is the invention of a scientific gentleman, named Stafford, who has secured a patent for the same. Before we give a description of the vehicle, it may be proper to state, that on the suggestion of the superintendant of the royal mails a similar coach, intended for the country was built, in order that its mechanical construction might be fully and practically tried and tested. Accordingly a public trial of one built at Nottingham was made, in presence of several hundreds of the most respectable inhabitants of that town. 1' risbv, an experienced and well-known whip, took the reins ; tlic coach was drawn by four spirited horses, and had, inside and out, the full compliment of passengers. In descending the hill to New Radford it was several times intentionally, when running at tire top of speed, suddenly swerved off the road, the near wheels working upon a bank three feet high, and the oil wheels in the drain. In each

Tarawirxajrt t&affaaraatst'Sta ATSS emergency the coach retained its vertical position like a mariner's compass, so much so that the gentlemen who composed the inside passengers were altogether insensible of their (to others) apparently perilous situation. þÿ The body of the new coach instead of resting, as is usually the case, upon springs below, is poised upon two upright supporters rising from the beds and axles, and passing up between the body and the boots. The tops of these supporters are surmounted by elliptic springs, on which the body is so suspended that on meeting inequalities on the road the centre of gravity of the vehicle is freely adjusted, and the liability to overturn is completely conquered.

The Terror was finally beached last Wednesday, and to look at her at low water, when you can walk round her, it is really surprising how she reached land, the whole of her keel, from the 10 footmark, being gone. The iron plates, which are nailed to secure the remnant of her "forefoot," when she was literally perched on the ice, are now apparent. The heavy sea which she encountered off Cape Farewell, on the south of Greenland shook her very much, more than anything since she left the ice. It is thought she may be sufficiently repaired to be towed round by a steamer to Plymouth.
