The Gorgon þÿ The following is the pithy and appropriate speech delivered by the Lady of Captain Superintendent Cumby, on the occasion of naming the Gorgon steam-frigate, when launched from Pembroke Dock-yard, on the 31st ult. ; þÿ " May good luck and success attend you þÿ commanded by British officers, and manned by British sailors, go forth and prosper. By the blessing of God, w hen opposed to the enemies of your Queen and country, you will do justice to the talent of your able and ingenious Architect." She then dashed the bottle of wine against the bows of the ship. The scene was very interesting. The Gorgon steam-frigate has arrived at Sheerncss from Pembroke, where she will be docked, and fitted with pipes and cocks preparatory to receiving her engines, of Bolton and Watt's manufacture, now ready in Woolwich Dock-yard. She will have two engines of 110 horse power each. This vessel is capable cf taking on board coals for fifteen days' consumption, and a regiment of the line, with the necessary provisions and water for their supply during that period, over and above her crew and armament, which latter consists of fourteen long 32- pounders and two 31 pounders, on circular sweeps. This splendid specimen of Naval architecture has excited universal admiration from every one who has had an opportunity of inspecting her form and capabilities. The Hague Oct. 12 þÿ The Royal Family and the whole country have this day been plunged in deep mourning by the death of her

under the effects of the malady Majesty the Queen, w ho this afternoon which bom sunk she had long been suffering, and which, within the last few days, had assumed the most alarming symptoms. The loss of this Princess, whose virtues and piety had long secured to her the love and esteem of the whole nation, will be a subject of very general grief, but above all the poor will have cause to deplore ment of one whose secret benefactions the bereave- had made them look on her with almost filial affection. Her Majesty Frcderica Louisa Wilhrlmina of Prussia was born on the 18th of November, 1774, audhad consequently nearly completed her 63d year. She was a daughter of King Frederik William the Second, and was married to the Prince ef Orange, our present King, on the 1st of October, 1791. The following is the official announcement of this melancholy event, as published in the Staats Courant of this : þÿ " It has pleased Divine Providence to take to Himself her Majesty the Queen, at a quarter before one o'clock this day. « During the latter part of Her Majesty's residence at the Loo she suffered from a progressive decay of strength, which, however, did not hinder her Majesty from returning to this place on the 4th of this month, but her strength continued to decline, and after having, especially since yesterday evening, rapidly grown worse, her Majesty expired without pain." One of his Majesty's aides-de-camp set off immediately for Berlin, to bear the melancholy tidings to the Prussian Court, and more

particularly to her late Majesty's daughter, the Princess- Albert of Prussia. The theatres and all places of amusement are to remain closed till further order, and B is expected, in consequence of the affliction which has befallen the country, that the opening of the session of the States General, on Monday next, will take place with as littie ceremony as possible, by one of the ministers in his Majesty's name.

With a strong and loyal body of Her Majesty's troops, and the wellorganised militia of Upper Canada, and the powerful assistance of H. M.s ships, we trust the rebellion will be crushed in its infancy. O'Connell lias addressed a long letter to the People of Ireland, the scope of which is to impress upon them the necessity of strenuously supporting the Queen's Government. But though this is the main object of his letter, O'Connell discourses on a variety of other subjects. He strenuously insists on the necessity " It is now manifest that the Reform Bill of the Ballot þÿ has not gone far enough in England or in Scotland. In the first place, take England. The Reform Bill excludes an enormous number of the people of England from the franchise. Can the excluded think this right or just ? 1 should despise them if they bore it patiently. Let them not waste their energies in abusing the Whigs or aiding the Tories, but let the misrepresented English rally and meet, and form Reform Associatisns, and signify to Parliament, by their petitions, their demand of the franchise. It seems to trie that all the people of England may, with Die greatest safety, be empowered to vote for Representatives. I deem it palpably unjust to call upon any man to pay any tux either directly or as part of the price of any necessary article, unless that man has a right to vote in the choice of the taxing representative. " When I see one class of Englishmen Comiug out of the hands of Nature superior in frame and in intellect to any other class, 1 will then, and not till then, admit that there ought to be a superior or master class, and an inferior or slave class in England; and that the first should be exclusively entitled to

participate in making the laws, and that the second should have nothing to do with the laws but to obey them. " But this slave class does exist in England. More shame for the English. " Our duty w ill be to vote for every extension of suffrage to the English People " We owe a similar duty to the People of Scotland. " The shortening the duration of Parliament to, at the utmost, three years, will be another duty. But the greatest of all is the Ballot. I must confess, that after the experience of the recent elections þÿ the intimidation, the bribery, the profligacy of the Tories at the late elections, rendering the Reform Bill, in many instances, worse than the old system of direct nomination þÿ after the failure of the Reform Bill, it seems to be scarcely credible that any honest and conscientious man can be an enemy to the Ballot. For my part, I candidly confess I cannot understand how a man can honestly desire to see the voters freely exercise their right of voting and yet oppose the Ballot, which at all events would leave them quite free to rote as they pleased. It may be said that in enormously large town constituencies, the Ballot, is not necessary ; yet even there it could be no harm, and would necessarily protect many. It may be said that jn very small constituencies, such, for example as Harwich þÿ it would not prevent wholesale bribery. But this is a strong argument against small constituencies, and not against the Ballot, because, is there any doubt that, without the Ballot, bribery prevails in Har-

wich? þÿ and even then the Ballot would render bribery more difficult to be eflected and more easy to be proved. In large constituencies the Ballot would render bribery almost impossible. I do, therefore, not hesitate to tell the People of Ireland to put but little faith in any man who does not vote for the Ballot."

( From the Nevis Post, December 12.) The attention of our readers are directed to the extract of a letter which will be found in our first page, from Mr. Doyle of the Island of Dominica, to the Editor of the 'Colonist' Newspaper of that Island, referring to the conduct of Lieutenant Owen of ller Majesty's Steamer Car run. It is unnecessary for us to comment on this subject, the thing speaks for itself þÿ for the sake of humanity we rejoice, that the curteous behaviour, and conciliating manners of Lieutenant Owen are not common to all Commanders of iier Majesty's vessels.

DOMINICA. To the admirers of expeditions and agreeable steam travelling, we recommend an attentive perusal of Mr Doyle's letter ; this Gentleman left Nevis on Thursday morning the 10th instant in the Steamer Carron, and was landed here on Thursday evening the 23rd instant, thus accomplishing this long voyage in the unusual short period of 7 days and 12 hours I It must not however be expected that all H. Majesty's Steamers are þÿ able to compete in velocity with the Carron, nor all H. M. Lieutenants exhibit the splendid hospitality and conciliating manners of the Cart on's commander.

(To the Editor of the Colonist ) Dear Sir, -I shall feel obliged by your affording space in your columns tor the following statement of facts which I deem it my duty to lay before the public. Being at Nevis and anxious to return hither w ith all speed, 1 embarked on Thursday the 16th Instant at 7 30 a. m , on board Her Majesty's Steamer Carron, commanded by Lieutenant Owen þÿ Shortly afterwards the Commander came on board, and at 8 o'clock proceeded for Montserrat, where we did not arrive till half past four þÿ at about 5 o'clock we departed for Antigea and reached English Harbour about 4 next morning þÿ at 7 the Commander appeared and stated that he should be detained three or four days, and that he could not accommodate his passengers during that time þÿ I enquired what was to be done? There was no Tavern or lodging house to be found, nor could we procure the smallest at tide of food or any place of shelter. þÿ The Commander replied we could hire a horse and gig and proceed to St. John's þÿ to this alternative we were obliged to resort and having remained four days at considerable expense, returned to English Harbour, when we were informed the Steamer could not go 'till the following þÿday thus we were exposed to be left without shelter for the night or food to sustain nature, which must have been the case hut for the great kindness of a resident gentleman (Mr. Brown) who rescued us from such a calamitv þÿ On Wednesday the 22nd instant, at 4 p. m., a gun was fired from the Steamer, when we pro-

ceeded on board, and at 5 she left this harbour for Guadaloupe; we reached Basseterre at 8 next morning and at 9 departed from this port where I was landed about 9 o'clock last evening. The Commander exacted and received from me an enormous sum of Ninety Spanish Dollars for the passage of myself and two Servants from Nevis to this place, a distance which is frequently accomplished by the ordinary sailing vessel in 21 hours þÿ hut this is not all ; both myselt and servants were nearly starved on þÿboard the latter were driven forward amongst the Coals, where they could but with difficulty find shelter, and 1 was thrust into a Berth the tloor of which was constantly covered with water, and over the Bed place the water came trickling down upon me somewhat in the manner of a shower hath, and finally on landing, the Commander required me to jump into the surf, threatened to throw my servant overboard, and eventually threw my luggage into the sea. The dreadful oaths continually made use ol by the Commander is another serious evil amongst the many horrors I could point out. 1 am Dear Sir, Yours very truly, THOMAS W. DOYLE.

LONDON, OCT. as. There are several indications that the Tory Opposition mean to give the Government little trouble in the early part of the ensuing session, except by their election petitions. It is not the cue of the Tories to seek any reduction of the Civil List which Ministers will propose ; rather would they bid high for Royal favour by voting an exorbitant income to the young Queen. Sir Robert Peel, we are informed, is not expected to return from the Continent till after Christmas. The Quarterly Review, published this week, warns the Tories against any premature assault on Downing Street. Lord Francis Egeuton, as likely as any member of the party to be in the secret of its tactics, talks mildly of " checking the evil measures of the Government." The Times lJost, and Standard , have lowered their tone of exultation : no loncer o promising an immediate overthrow of the Whigs. From all these symptoms, it appears that the Tory policy is to hold back and gather additional strength The calculation is, that on the whole of the election petitions, at least six seats will be lost by the Liberals, counting twelve votes in the division ; and the Tories will make strenuous efforts to substitute their own men for Liberals when single vacancies occur. It is undeniable that by this process the small Ministerial majority may be gradually overbalanced : the Ministers, defeated in the House of Commons, may be compelled to resign, and another dissolution take place with the l ories in power. That such will be the course of

politics, is too likely, unless a change is made m the Liberal tactics. The Tories are marching on the Cabinet as surely and safely as a besieging army on a fortress, whose garrison is too weak or too cowardly to disturb the operations of the assailants by a sally or a shell. Daily the defences are cut down, and the mine advances. Preparations for the final onslaught are made under the eyes of the beleaguered troops ; and yet not a trumpet is sounded or a war cry raised within the walls. There are brave men in the fortress, eager for action ; but their officers look coldly upon them, and deem their desire to engage the enemy as a proof <>f treachery. Time will show who are the real traitors. þÿ Spectator.

ENGLAND. return of members. Confining ourselves to England, it will astonish our readers to find how very small a portion of the population returns the Tory members. In the first place, of the boroughs with a population of 100,000 and upwards þÿ namely, the Tower Hamlets, Finsburv, Maryla-bone, Westminster, London city, Lambeth, Southwark, Liverpool, Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, the only one which returned Tories is Liverpool. Giving Liverpool to the Tories, we have of towns with 100,000 inhabitants and upwards, a population returning Reformers of 1,820,000, and only 103,000 returning Tories. Descending to the class of boroughs with a population of from 50,000 to 100,000, and in case of towns which return one of each party, placing half the population to the account of the Reformers and half to the account of the Tories, we have Sheffield, Portsmouth, Greenwich, Norwich, Newcastle, Nottingham, Bristol, Bath, Wolverhampton, Stoke upon Trent, and Sallbrd. Of these towns a population of 431,000 returns Reformers, and only 275,000 Tories. Of the boroughs with a population of from 20,000 to 50,000 Reformers, are returned by 730,000 inhabitants, and Tories, by 300,700. But when we descend to the smaller boroughs, of which a part of the electors can be bribed or intimidated, the case begins to alter. Of the boroughs with a population of from 10, 000, to 20,000, a population of 331,000 re turns Reformers, and 330,000 returns Tories. Of the next class of boroughs with a population under 10,000,305,100 inhabitants return

Reformers and 272,500 return Tories. The general result is, that a population of 3,032, 000 returns Reformers, and of 1,385,000 returns Tories The most bigoited Tory will not deny that there is more intelligence and independence in the towns than in the counties, and more in large towns than in small. Taken by this tost, Ministers have the support of an overwhelming majority of the enlightened and independent inhabitants of England. In boroughs with 100,000 inhabitants and upwards, the Liberal is to the Tory population as 95 to 10. In boroughs with 10,000 inhabitants and upwards, the Liberal is to the Tory population as 39 to 10. And in the whole boroughs collectively, the Liberal is to the Tory population as 20 to 10. Ministers have consequently a good working majority Parliament, backed by 3 in to 1 of the town population of England. The Tory minority represents therefore but a very small proportion of the town population of England, the only population that can manifest independent opinion. þÿ Watchman , October 25.

Cure for the Yellow Fever. þÿ The following efficacious method of treating the Yellow Fever, appears to have been practised with success, by the late Ferdinand Smith Stuart, M. D. As it appears to be a rational, and at the same time a simple process, it is made public with a view to serve mankind ; and in the hope that it may he the means, under Providence, of saving many valuable lives, who otherwise might become the victims of that dreadful and generally fatal disease. It is extracted from Memoirs of l)r F. S Stuart, published in the London Monthly Magazine for February 1815: þÿ "In his voyage to S't Domingo, the Doctor was wrecked three times in Admiral Christian's fleet, in 1795 and 1796, above live thousand men being lost, and not one-sixth of four hundred sail returned to England. þÿ He was afterwards at the capture of St. Lucia, at Martinique, and again in St. Domingo, when 7600 British troops, and as many seamen, died in five weeks of the yellow' fever, which, though not of the medical staff; he discovered the means of alleviating or curing. þÿ All the remedies prescribed by impudent empirics (savs Dr. S) are the basest falsehoods and impositions ; for the disease is

merely a bilious fever, with the bile rendered acrid and corrosive by the extreme heat, "and is cured by five grains of tartarised antimony, and one table spoonful of soft sugar, dissolved in fifteen table spoonluls of boiling water, of which one is taken every fifteen or twenty minutes, until it has operated three distinct times, when an immense quantity of acrid thick viscid bile is evacuated, and the patient immediately relieved ; toast and water with nitre is used for constant drink, and one ounce of nitrom vitriolalum (Glauber's salts) takes in it on the second and third day after, which, with bark in Port wine during a state of convalescence, lias constantly completed the recovery."

From the St. Thomas Times, December 20. LOWER CANADA. From the Halifax Journal, Nov 6. Our intelligence from Lower Canada still continues, to be of an unpleasant nature. The Quebec Papers received here are to the 23rd ult., on which day it is said a meeting of the inhabitants of live extensive Counties was to be held for rebellious principles, and a letter from Quebec of the same date, which we have seen, states that apprehensions were entertained that the Independence of the same Counties would be declared, and that prompt, strong, and decisive measures, on the part of the Government, would be necessary to oppose so revolutionary a proceeding. We are happy to see in the Montreal papers of Tuesday a requisition calling a Public meeting, to be held on Monday next, the 23d instant. The loyal requisition to which we allude is followed by 020 names, and is couched in the following terms : þÿ ' The undersigned request a meeting of their fellow citizens to be held on Monday at the Place d'Armes, at twelve o'clock (noon)' to take into their serious consideration the measures which, in the present crisis, it may be found necessary to adopt, to maintain good order, the protection of lite and property, and the connexion now happily existing between this Colony and the British Kingdom, at present put in jeopardy by the machinations of a disorganising and revolutionary faction within this Province, professedly bent on their destruction." On this subject, the Herald has the following editorial remarks : þÿ " We publish to day the requisition for a

public Meeting of the Citizens for Monday next. We are to state, as an example of the great enthusiasm which prevails among the "British and Irish inhabitants, that all the names published to day were obtained during the afternoon of yesterday. We shall publish additional signatures to-morrow. P. S. þÿ In the Herald of Wednesday the number of signatures is increased to 1257.

From the West Indian, Dec. 7. On Monday next, according to the Vindicator and Minerve, the standard of revolt is to be openly raised at St. Charles, and a Canadian declaration of Independence sworn to. The Canadians come to the meetings with muskets on their shoulders. Military exercises are much attended to. Paragraphs, like the following, from the last Vindicator, may serve to show that the Canadians are serious : " The different Sections of the ' Sons of Liberty,' mustered in considerably strength, on Sunday afternoon, at Cote-au, St. Louis, on the farm of the Hon. L). B. Viger, in the rear of the Bishop's Church. There could not have been less than twelve hundred effective men embodied. They were put through the different military evolutions, with much credit to themselves, considering the short time the corps has been under drill.

From the New Orleans Bulletin. DISTRESSING STEAM BOAT ACCIþÿDENT THREE HUNDRED LIVES LOST. New Orleans, Nov, 3d. þÿ Another dreadful accident has occurred upon our wateis, which have lately become the scene of so rrany heart-rending and appalling catastrophes. The steamer Monmouth left this port about a week since, laden with several hundred In dians, a portion of the Creek tribe, as pas. sengers. In travelling up the Missisippi, through Prophet Island Bend, she was met by the ship Trenton, in tow by the steamer Warren, descending the river It was after dark, being near eight o'clock at night, and through the mismanagement of the officers, and tiie obscurity of the scene, a collision took place between the meeting vessels, and the Monmouth immediately sunk from the violence of the concussion. Out of the large number ol Indians on board, near three hundred perished Whether any of the crew were saved or not we have not learned. The mishap is ascribed chiefly to the neglect of the officers of the Monmouth. She was running in a part of the stream where, by tlie usages of the river, and the rules of the Mississippi navigation, site had no right to go, and where of course, the descending tow did not expect to meet her. Here is another evidence of the gross carelessness of a class of men to whose charge we often commit our personal safety and precious lives. From the True American. The fearful responsibility of this vast sacrifice of human life rests on the contractors for emigrating the Creek Indians. The

avaricious disposition to increase the profits of the speculation first induced the chartering of rotten, old, and unseaworthy boats, because they were of a class to be procured cheaply : and then to make those increased profits still larger, the Indians were packed upon these crazy vessels in such crowds, that not the slightest regard seems to have been paid to their safety, comfort, or even decency. The crammed condition of the decks and cabins was offensive to every sense and feeling, and kept the poor creatures in a state unfit for human beings Six hundred were jammed into this boat, (the Monmouth,) and three hundred of them have perished.

The Wealth of England. þÿ It is a common errof in this country to imagine that the riches of England are derived from, and are dependent upon, her commerce ; the influence of this great mistake is shown in the many wild suppositions that have been hazarded, touching the eflcci of our commercial and financial difficulties upon the financial and political condition of the wonderful little island. The truth is, that the merchants of England, with all their great capital and vast extent of operations, hold but a very small portion of t he riches existing in the country ; and this truth can be made apparent bv a few simple considerations. Look at the squirearchy, for instance ; the thousands and thousands of country gentlemen, with their comfortable incomes of three or five or ten thousand pounds per annum, derived exclusively from the soil ; and the enormous fortunes of the nobility. Estimate, if it can be estimated, the immense amount of treasure in the country, existing in the form of plate and jewels. þÿ Why, at a single dintici ,:ven in Loudon on the 19th of June, gold and silver plate to the value of a million and a half of dollars, was exhibited at once; all the property of one individual þÿ the Duke of Wellington. That celebrated personage could have relieved from their difficulties all three of the great American houses which have been compelled to stop, simply by turning over to them his dishes, tureens, and vases, and candtdebras, without diminishing his income by a farthing ; and there are fifty

noble ladies in London, any one of whom might have put the Messrs. Brown & Co. in ample funds for all emergencies, merely by making them a present of Iter diamonds. Without taking the crown jewels into the account, it is no doubt susceptible of proof that in London alone, there are gold and silver plate and jewels to the amount of two hundred millions of dollars ; and it must be remembered that mighty as is London, the wealth of the kingdom in wrought gold and silver, is very far from being centered there. An immense quantity of it is scattered among the castles and country seats of the nobility, such as Alnwick Castle, Blenheim, Chatwortli, Belvoir, Wobutti Abbey, Bowood, and a hundred others which we could name, and among the lovely mansions of the coutry gentlemen, with which the whole surface of thts island is dotted in thousands. Then think of the libraries and þÿgalleries the immense and almost priceless collections ol

pictures and statues, and other costly Works of art, in which no country in the wot Id is richer. Why, the whole mercantile wealth of England is but an item in her riches þÿ a mere item, of comparatively trifling magnitude. The non payment of our debt, il it were not paid, which, thank Heaven, it soon will be, so far from inflicting a mortal blow upon the prosperity of the kingdom, would never be felt or though of except as a handy theme for a sarcasm now and then, directed against republican honesty and honor. '1 he fortune of the Duke ol Bedford, or Northumberland, or Devonshire, would clear oil the whole of it, and nobody but bis grace be anything the poorer. New York Commercial Advertiser.

Of course he passed while on board as a subordinate individual ol his Minister s retinue and separating himself from the ceremonious group, he found his amusement in wandering alone among the seamen, and throughout the vessel, inquiring and conversing with the utmost freedom. Commodore Nicholson, however, aware of the disguise, directed a salute of forty one guns to be fired as soon as lie returned to his steamer, and finding himself thus discovrcd and announced, his Majesty hoisted the American ensign, gave signals to his principal ship of war in our neighborhood for a return ol our salute, and

The earth contains no poison, the air no pestilence, which providence has not at the same time endowed with some principle which mankind will, some day or another, turn to use. All is not, indeed, discovered at once ; but let us look at the most deleterious substance known in nature or m art, and see the murderous arsenic, how useful it is in hardening t\pes, and thus ministering to a press; in forming specula lor reflecting telescopes ; in making glass ; in dyeing ; in printing cotton stuffs ; nay, in pharmacy as a tonic. Man is a rational being ; hut man is also and much more, a passionate being þÿ his reason bearing, perhaps the same proportion to his passion, as the oxygen bears to the azote in the common atmospheric air. The utmost that man's reason has yet done for him, is to aid him in subduing his brute creation to his obedience, and to give him some slight power over the elements, so as in a measure to make the wind his messengers, and the flaming lire his servant ; but he holds by his reason no dominion over passion. In arithmetic and men. suration he is perfectly rational ; but in morals and politics the animal outweighs and out measures the rational.

The keeping of one day in seven holy, as a relaxation and refreshment, as well as for public worship, is of admirable service to a state, considered merely as a civil institution. It humanises, by the help of society and conversation, the manners of the lower classes, which would otherwise degenerate into a sordid ferocity and savage 'selfishness of spiiit ; il enables the industrious workman to puisue his occupation, in the ensuing week, with health and cheerfulness ; it imprints on ihe minds of the people that sense of their duty to God so necessary to make them good citizens, þÿ but yet which would be worn out and defaced by an unremitting continuance of labour without any stated time for calling them ttf the worship of their Maker. þÿ Blachstone.

Shading the Eyes. Some people cover their eyes with green or other shades when any thing is the matter with them. This is wrong. It is now ascertained by the best oculists that shades injure the sight instead of strengthening it, and thus from these creaiing heat and inflammation in the parts artecied- If the eye be injured, and light insupportable, the best way is to tie a cool linen handkerchief over it. We have heard it stated as a curious fact, that when the English army returned from Egypt, those soldiers were least aflected with opthalmia þÿ a disease in the eyes þÿ who had worn no snouts to their hats. The eyes evidently require to be played upon by a free circulation of air, and therefore broad brimmed bats may be said to be any thing but protectors to the organs of vision, for the heat radiates from ihe ground more than from the sun overhead. It is worthy of notice, that none of the natives of hot climates wear head coverings with snouts or brims ; and we should think that they were good judges in these matters.

From the Montreal Gazette, October 7. We have this day the pleasure of submitting to the perusal of our readers an Address to the Queen, from the inhabitants of this city and neighbourhood, and which, it is proposed to lay before the public on Monday for subscription. TO THE QUEEN'S MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY. Most Gracious Sovereign, We, your þÿMajesty most s dutiful and loyal subjects, inhabitants of the Province of Lower Canada, respectfully approach your Koval presence with the expression of our sincere condolence, on the severe aflliction which your Majesty, in common with the whole British Empire, has sustained by the dectase of our lamented and beloved King. We respectfully entreat permission to tender to your Majesty our heartfelt congratulations upon your þÿMajesty saccession to the Throne of your ancestors, the assurance of

person and Government, and our sincere and ardent wishes that your þÿMajesty reign s may be long and prosperous, supported bv the affections of grateful subjects, arid rewarded by the union and happiness of a loyal and devoted people. Animated with these sentiments, we deplore necessity the which compels us, at this particular period, approach your Majesty to with aught but the most hearty expressions of our confidence in your þÿMajesty s anxious desire to promote the welfare and happiness of your Majesty's subjects, but the critical posture of affairs in this remote Colony, aftcetmg alike the prosperity of the Colony, its connexion with your þÿMajesty Government, s and the integrity of the Empire, forces us most reluctantly to address your Majesty in the language of supplication for relief from unjust oppression, and redress from unmerited grievances. By a series of munificent benefactions bestowed upon the Colony, by the bountiful liberality your þÿMajesty predecessors, of s to a degree of political profusion, surpassing the most sanguine expectations, and comprehending the full exercise of religious worship, perfect security of person and property, the almost universal suffrage for all classes, the constitution of a representative Government, and complete immunity from external taxation, granted to all the Colonists, and the free enjoyment of tlreir ancient laws, specially preserved to the inhabitants of French origin, and by the division of the Province of Quebec

into two separate Governments, with a local Legislature established in each, the prosperity of this favored Province was confidently believed to have been sacred, and the most effectual means afforded of extinguishing competition and national prejudices among the inhabitants of different origin, and of forming them into one happy and united people Possessing these enviable civil and political advantages, enjoying moreover an impartial administration of justice, and subjected to a mild and beneficent Government, it might have been hoped that separate interests would have merged into the liberty and security of all the Colonists, without distinction of origin , but this lias not been the case, and experience lias demonstrated the political inexpediency of that Provincial division, which has continued the existence of the inhabitants of French origin as a distinct people, essentially different from their fellow-subjects of British

a»Asrss: TOimiraasx ®a®aa»asr»s ATas. origin, and has cultivated among them a spirit of hostility to British connexion, and a delusion respecting their national independence, which lias grown with the increase of their numerical population. The evil consequences resulting from this unfortunate distinction of origin, are exhibited in Lower Canada, in the opposition and hostility of the political leaders of the inhabitants of French origin, to every measure lending to increase British capital or British population in the Province, or to aflord to the inhabitnnts of British origin a fair share in the Provincial representation, and in their unceasing endeavours to destroy the Constitution, and to introduce a republican form of government in its stead, while their culpable disinclination, or absolute refusal to second the improvements in progress in Upper Canada, for increasing the prosperity of both Provinces, and for facilitating their mutual intercourse, and their jealousy of the great improvement and aggrandizement of that Province, piove our loyalty and devotion to your Majesty's I that similar consequences have extended their influence beyond the limits of Lower Canada. Under the fostering protection of the Imperial Government, the commerce, wealth, and population of Lower Canada have greatly increased, the latter to an extent ten fold its original number at the time of the conquest, of whom about 400,000 are of French origin, and more than 200,000 of British origin, while the actual population of Upper I

Canada, amounting to nearly 400,000, is rapidly increasing in a degree far exceeding that of Lower Canada. By means of public meetings held in various parts of Lower Canada, at which the most unfounded and inflammatory speeches have been delivered, the political leaders of the inhabitants of French origin have endeavoured to excite the mass of that population to a disregard of the laws, attempts to obstruct their operation, to mockery of religion, to insubordination and sedition, and every artifice is employed, with daily increasing boldness, to render them discontented with your Majesty's Government and disobedient to the laws to seduce them from their allegiance to their Sovereign, and finally to bring about a rebellion, in which the prosperity and internal happiness of the Colony must be eventually sacrificed. We have long and patiently borne our j grievances, in tlic confident hope that our exertions to maintain order, and to support the due execution of the law, our attachment to j the Constitution of the Province and solicitude to preserve the connexion of the Colony, w ith the Parent State, and our consistent loyalty would be fully appreciated. We most respectfully urge upon your Maþÿjesty s attention, that the period so long so earnestly desired has at length arrived, when national distinctions among the Colonists may be forever extinguished, the evil consequences of the Provincial division extirpated, and the necessity for measures of coercive severi-

ty altogether avoided ; and that these advantages can only be attained by the Legislative Union of the Provinces a measure w hich has already been submitted to the consideration of your þÿMajesty s predecessors, and which must inevitably take place at some future period, when the difficulties in the way of its accomplishment shall have been greatly enhanced. In support of this important measure, it is unnecessary to advert to the geographical J

situation of the Provinces, and their possession of hut one outlet to the sea, the collection by one Province alone of the revenue of both, and the extreme difficulty of adjusting the proportion of the general revenue for each, but we most confidently appeal to the fact, that neither Province was expressly reserved for the settlement of the inhabitants of one race alone, to the professed intention of the Provincial di\ision, and to its utter failure after the experience of nearly fifty years, as the most conclusive reason in support of the Legislative Union of the Provinces of Lower Canada and Upper Canada. We earnestly solicit your þÿMajesty consi- s deration to the redress of ihose grievances, which most injuriously affect us as inhabitants of LowerCanada, the continuance of the feudal tenure in the Seignorial parts of the Province, the want of an efficient Registration for Mortgages, and our absolute exclusion from a just share in the Representation of the Province ; expediency, policy and justice unite in requiring a commutation of the feudal tenure, by which land may be transmitted from hand to hand relieved from its present incumbrances, and free from the imposition of a heavy tax upon improvement ; the establishment of a genera! system of registration for mortgages, by which security may he afforded for the investment of capital, and the existing facilities for fraud and dishonesty in that respect prevented, and a new division of Counties in Lower Canada by w hich our interests

may be provided for by a due proportion of Representation according to our just rights, and our numbers, wealth and intelligence, and a participation afforded to us in the privileges of a Representative Government, granted to all the inhabitants of the Province without distinction of origin, hut from whose benefits, we are virtually excluded by the division of counties now in force : and while we humbly declare to your Majesty our sincere conviction that unless your Majesty, assisted by the wisdom of the Imperial Parliament, shall accomplish these important remedial measures, there exists no probability of their being carried into effect by the Provincial Legislature as at present constituted, we cannot conceal from your Majesty that a longer delay in their completion will produce uneasiness and apprehension in the minds of your þÿMajesty loyal s Provincial subjects. Cordially participating in those feelings o4 devotion which pervade all classes throughout the Empire, we most earnestly pray that your Majesty may be lorg preserved to reign with glory over a devoted and united people, and that every blessing may be abundantly poured forth ujioii your Majesty and your Royal House þÿ Montreal, September 20, 137. þÿ þÿ -<X Fromthe Barbadian, December 1C, 1837.

About the time of sunset last evening Her Majesty's Packet Lapwing, came to anchor in Carlisle Bay, 28 days passage from Falmouth. We received our London files (Lis morning. The only very interesting int'-lligence related in these papers is, the glorious and imposing procession of her gracious Majesty to the renowned City of London, and the magnificent and sumptuous Banquet in honour ol her Majesty's condescending visit to the Civic authorities, on Lord Mayor's Hay. The ceremonial is described at great length, occupying 10 columns of a double sheet of the Evening Mail, The splendour ol the illuminations, the gorgeous parade

JE>A5T3:£ through the immensely crowded streets of the Citv, from Temple Bar to Guildhall, the presence of lloyality, and the first nobility of the land, and the profuse, luxuriant banquet under which the tables groaned, must have presented a scene of magnificence, and grandeur, which no commercial city in the world> except London, could ever exhibit. þÿ We do not know (says the Editor of Hell's Weekly Messenger) any circumstance which ought to afford more unqualified satisfaction to every thinking man, who has the interest of his country at heart, and who earnestly desires the maintenance of all her monarchical institutions, than, in the first place, the kind and wise consideration of the youthful Queen in cherishing the good feelings of her subjects by a procession suitable to the splendour of the great monarchy over which she presides ; and, in the second, the warm and generous return which has every where been made to her royal courtesy. It is a known property in human nature, that our feelings and affections like our bodily faculties, are confirmed and increased by being exercised, and, that therefore, the best way of producing and increasing loyal feelings, is, that of affording the most frequent occasions of exercising them It was, therefore, sound prudence, as well as right feeling, in our young and ingenious Queen, when, in answer to the invitation of the City, she returned not only a formal, but a hearty acquiescence, þÿ and, according to every credible report, looked forward to the day as

no less a day of enjoyment to herself than of gratification to every class of her subjects ', The public mind, besides the excitement caused by the splendid pageant of the Oth November, had been greatly agitated by a shameful þÿpersona outrage on the Queen by an Officer, a Captain Goode, of the Hussars, as well as by an attempt to take her life and that of her Boyal mother, by a German of the name of Stuber. Both individuals, doubtless insane persons, were apprehended, and the circumstances investigated. We have not room to-day for the particulars ol these interesting occurrences. Her Majesty was pleased to confer the honour of a Baronetcy on the Bight Honorable John Gowan, the new Lord Mayor, and to bestow the honour of Knighthood on the two Sheriffs, Mr John Carrol, and Mr. Moses Montefiore. þÿ1 helatter gentleman is a Je w, and is said to be the first person of that religious persuasion who has been thus highly honoured. The civic banquet was graced by the company of noblemen and gentlemen of all political parties, who all partook in the general happiness, and vied with each other in demonstialions ol loyalty and attachment to their amiable young Sovereign. Her Majesty, it is said, drank wine to fifteen different parties þÿ of course only going through the motion, merely raising the glass to her lips, which wc dare say, were as þÿ ruby þÿred, as the wine it contained. When her Majesty drank to the Lord Mayor's health, we are told it was in Sherry, of one hundred and twenty years old It makes

one's lips water to think of such a bonne louche, which we sholud not much dislike to have handed to our wine-loving lips þÿ what a delicious sangaree it would make, provided it lias not lost its flavour from its extreme antiquity, þÿ which we should rather apprehend, though, probably, the Queen did riot find that out. Our only extract to-day from the London papers is, the short account of the meeting of the House of Commons on the loth Novem-

Oriental Fable. þÿ The following apologue is translated from some German author, but wc arc not informed of bis name. It is eminently beautilul, and cannot be read without pleasure and advantage : þÿ þÿ At a court of the caliph Musa A1 Hadi, lived an old man, by name A1 Baschid, on whom the petty courtiers exercised their wit, whom the ladies disliked, and who, during seventy six years, had been fourteen times banished from the presence of his sovereign, because some unpleasant truth was forever dropping from bis lips. He laughed at banishment, for, in the garden of nature, he always found the best company; and the court fourteen times recalled him, because it was conceived be could be happy at a distance from court. During one of the period of his punishment, as he was tracing the path of wisdom in rctircm''nt, he was lucky enough to gain a knowledge in the language of animals. From that moment, bi-s favorite aiwre-

ATH3 þÿ þÿ þÿtg þÿ1 þÿ merit was in listening to them, and lie fouhti that they often talked more rationally than the great men who surrounded the caliph s throne lie one day observed upon the leaves of a bush a colony of those insects called ephemera ; to whom the Creator has affixed the end of their existence almost close to the hour of their birth þÿ for they arc borrt and die in the same day. þÿ A1 Baschid attentively approached a small group of them, and perceived they were engaged in a violent dispute; but as they were all talking together, it was long bclore he could discover the subject of their controversy. At length when the most vociferous among them had bawled out till tliev were tired, be tound that their conversation turned upon two toreign virtuosos, who were just arrived. These were a humble-bee and gnat, upon whose pre-endnence the opinions of the ephemera were much divided. One side maintained that the humble-bee sung the finest bass which had ever been heard throughout the temple of insects while the other defended the fascinating treble of the gnat. þÿ þÿ Happy race I exclaimed A1 Baschid, 1 who, in spite of the few hours allotted to their existence, can thus amuse yourselves with the bass of a bee or the treble of a þÿgnat. With a smile he turned his car to one of the oldest ephemera, who sat alone upon a leaf, and cele- tered the following soliloquy : The most utbrated philosophers of our nation, who lived many hours before me, have asserted that this

world cannot last longer than eighteen hours, and metliinks they were right ; for, when I , consider how much that great globe of fire from which all nature gains existence, has, even during my time, declined towards the sea which surrounds this earth, I cannot but suppose that it will there end its career, and its torch be extinguished in the waves. I fie earth must then be lost in total darkness, which must naturally produce universal annihilation. Of these eighteen hours I have lived seven þÿ four hundred & twenty minutes. A great age! How few among us reach this period ! I I have seen whole generations rise, flourish, and decay. My present friends are the children and grandchildren of those whom I knew in my youth. They are gone long before me, and, alas ! but too soon shall 1 follow them. I must own þÿ God be thanked I I feel tolerably well in my old age ; yet according to the customary course of nature, I can, at the very utmost, only expect to live I eighty minutes more. What then, avails all my industry ? What avails it that, with a thousand anxieties and cares, I have gathered a provision of sweet devv upon this leaf, which the approaching end of my existence will not allow me to enjoy 1 In vain have I, far from the bustle of the world, endeavored to form this colony by salutary þÿprecepts. þÿ Tis true my friends flatter me that I shall leave a great name behind me ; but, what avails this, if, at the end of eighteen hours, the sun shall be extinguished, and the world

dissolve into eternal nothingness? Oh, if I could but expect a durable fame for thirty or forty hours þÿ! þÿ Al Baschid smiled ; and immediately started at having smiled : þÿ for hours and years are they not the same at last !'

Quick Work. þÿ A Glasgow, Scotland paper, states that Bailie Clarkson, of Selkirk, sat down to dinner in a pair of inexpressibles made of wool, which that very same morning was growing on the hack of the sheep. In the brief space of eleven hours and a half, the fleece was shorn from the animal, scoured, dyed, carded, spun, woven, and made into a pair of breeches for Bailie !

Hint to Epicures. þÿ The teeth of Indians seldom decay, excepting in some slight degree by age þÿ and the cause may be referred to the pure and simple nature of their food þÿ taking nothing which can injure their teeth þÿ and none of what are called luxuries of j life. For the same reason, the hair of the | Indian, or of the white man, of the lower classes, seldom comes off-þÿ and we see many aged men with heads of thick and handsome hair. High living has a great influence in I Waistcoating, white and brown decaying the human system.

LATEST FROM UPPER CAjVADA. We hasten to communicate the important intelligence from Upper Canada, reccivdd by the Northern mail of this morning. would have been little

to them in the upper province. Some of the royal militia would not obey the government orders to turn out, and few volunteered, such was the general panic. The Comet. þÿ Is it not a grand and vast conception that this wan and misty orb has been travelling swifter than the swiftest cannon ball, through the dim realms of space, since our Saviour slept in the manger at Bethlehem, and the star in the cast lit its fires for the wise þÿmen eyes s ? Is it not like Divinity, that power of Astronomic prophecy, which pierced the curtains of the future and foretold the advent of this blazing world ? þÿ And when this generation shall be slumbering in the dust, that predicted orb will again stream its horrid þÿhair across our sky. þÿ No. 3 Mackerel, When the lover who has now looked at it I with his mistress shall become a patriarch among his children ; when the child now lisping its early enquiries of the wandering star, shall tell the tale in after years, to some | opposition, of moment, | grand-babe, throned on her þÿknee then the

comet will come again! What þÿchanges what revolutions þÿ what convulsions of states and empires þÿ will chance ere then ! lMy soul expands into a sense of sublimity, as 1 reflect on the vast world of events between, flow many ties will be severed þÿ how many hearts be broken þÿ how many tears he shed ! Yet while on earth these vicissitudes will advene and vanish, in that far element above and around us, this luminous globe shall winder with its þÿtrain flashing and glowing through the fields of immensity. Thought itself þÿ imagination in her boldest flight þÿ sinks with wearied wing, unable to grasp the stupendous, boundless theme ! Truly said the ancient minstrel : þÿ When I survey the heavens, the work of thy fingers þÿ the moon and the stars which thou hast ordained þÿ then 1 say, what is man, that thou art mindful of him, the or son of man that thou visitest him.

Brewster's Proposal to Map the Moon. In a letter addressed to me by Sir David Brewster, on occasion of our proposing to erect a new and splendidly-furnished observatory in Glasgow, is the following interesting paragraph ; þÿ To such an observatory, where the finest achromatic might be accompanied with a better reflecting telescope than has yet been made, it would be a leading object to delineate with percision the hills and vallies of the moon. This planet is much within our reach ; and an accurate knowledge of the phenomena it presents, and of the changes these undergo, would be a great and most interesting contribution to science. When we compare the telescope in þÿNewton s time to that ofSir William þÿHerschel s, we need scarcely despair of discovering the structures erected by the inhabitants of that luminary. An achromatic object glass of the same size as the sperulum ofSir William þÿHerschel s forty feet telescope, would certainly accomplish tins ; and no person can say that it is impracticable to do in glass what we have done in metal. Had 1 the means, I would not scruple to undertake the task of building the lens in zones and þÿsegments1 For the honour of British science, it is to be hoped that the power of accomplishing what would immortalize his age, will in some way be afforded to this distinguished þÿphilosopher þÿ jStchol's Architecture of the Heavens.

LONDON. Parliamenta ry intelligence. House of Commons þÿ Nov. 15. The House met at 2 o'clock this afternoon, Mr. I ,ey, the chief clerk of the House, taking the chair by the side of lite table. After lite Commons had returned from the House of Lords, to which they were summoned to hear the reading of Her Majesty's Commission opening the present session of Parliament, they proceeded to the election of Speaker. Mr- Shaw Lefevre, in a neat speech, in which he eulogized the excellent manner which the Eight Hon. James Abercrombie had performed all the arduous duties of Speaker during the last three sessions of parliament, proposed the re-election of that gentleman to the chair. Mr. Strutt seconded the motion, and laid particular stress on the praise which Mr. Abercrombie merited for the improvements which he bad introduced, and for the further improvements which be meditated, upon the mode of transacting the private business of the house. (Cheers) Sir R. Peel rose for the mere purpose of stating that he did not intend to give the slightest opposition to the proposal which had been made and seconded by the two lion, members who preceded him, considering the special circumstances in which the house was placed þÿ considering also that in the event of a contest, a majority þÿ a small majority, but still a majority (hear, hear) þÿ would decide in favour of the claims of Mr. Abcrcrombie þÿ considering, also, the personal respect which he had felt for that right hon. gentleman, even when he was a candidate for the chair in opposition to his noble friend

Lord Canterbury, and which he still continued to feel, he should cheerfully acquiesce in the proposition for replacing the right hon member for Edinburgh in the chair. (Hear, hear.) Air. Abercrombie made a few observations on the duties which the Speaker had to fulfil, his own incapacity to fulfil those duties adequately and his readiness to submit himself upon this as well as on ail other occasions to the decision of the House. There being no opposition to the election of Mr. Abercrombie, he was handed to the chair by his mover and seconded both sides of the House rising and remaining uncovered whilst he took it. The Speaker then addressed the house in the following terms: þÿ " To be placed in his chair under any circumstances is a high and distinguished honor. To be replaced in it after filling it for three years, and that too by an unanimous vote of the house, is an honour which 1 shall always esteem and cherish most highly. The only expression of gratitude which I presume to make is this, that 1 resume my place in this chair most firmly and zealously desirous to merit the confidence and support of those who placed me in it. Lord J. Russell, in moving the adjournment of the house congratulated Mr. Abercrombie on having been again elected to fill the olfice of Speaker. He felt confident that the election of Mr. Abercrombie to the chair without opposition would tend to the 'settlement ol many questions on which the experience ol the speaker was necessary, to the im-
provement of the mode of conducting the private business of the house, and if he (Mr. Abercrombic) were enabled thus to serve the country, he might congratulate himself that

whilst the house had on him conferred the honour of presiding over its deliberations, lie had by bringing to perfection those regulations which lie meditated, the opportunity of making the house more endeared to the country at large, and he would thus return to the house, in increased honor and estimation, the honour which it had so signally conferred upon him : and on which he (L.ord John Russell) again sincerely and cordially congratulated him. (Cheers) þÿ St. Thomas Times, Dec. 27.

LATF.lt FROM CANADA. Daily Commercial Advertiser, Extra. Buffalo, Saturday, Nov 9. The following communication was handed in this afternoon. It will be seen to be pretty highly colored by the writei's loyal notions, but its statement of facts can probably be relied upon, and, as it gees a more full and particular account of the recent events at Toronto than has yet appeared, we are induced to make it public. Buffalo, Saturday, 4 P. M. To the Editors of the Daily Com. Adv. Gentlemen þÿ Having arrived here last evening, from Toronto, (which place 1 left yesterday morning,) and being surprised at the statement iiere, 1 take the liberty of giving you the facts, as 1 am acquainted with every tiling that has taken place there within the last few days. The first symptoms of disturbances at Toronto occurred on Monday evening, when it was discovered by the burning ol Dr. Thorn's house, and by several who had been taken prisoners and escaped, that the rebels, to a considerable number, armed with l ilies, spears, <Slc, and headed by Alc'iveuzie, hail advanced to within two miles and a half of the city, proposing, as they have since declared, to lake the city, rob the banks, and set it oil lire. But the citizens, by this time being alarmed, armed thtmselves as they best could, and advanced to meet them, upon winch the rebels retreated upon Yonge street, as far as Montgomery's, about 5 miles out, and there made their head quarters. It must be understood that Toronto was at this time in a de-

fenceless condition þÿ the whole of the troops having left some time ago for Lower Canada ; but no time was lost, and never was a more animated scene than Toronto presented. þÿ The From all parts of the city the loyal, (both retormcrs and tories,) were collecting together, to receive arms and to concert measures for the defence of their wives, their children and their sacred homes against an infuriated and vicious rabble, led on by a bad, designing and disappointed mail. Orders were immediately issued by proclamation from the Adjutant General's otlice, for the militia to assemble under their colonels, and a cull made on all lite loyal men to assemble lor the defence ol their " C|ueen, country, arid constitution," and nobly was live call responded to. Old and young Hocked to the standard of their country, by hun-

dreds Steamboats w ere sent off to Hamilton and Niagara for militia n nd volunteers þÿ the Hon. Speaker Mc'Nab afteiward the commander, left Hamilton at the head of about 200 volunteers, on board the steamboat Burlington, on Wednesday morning, and Col. Chisholin. with as many militia, a few hours after in a schooner. Messrs. Hamilton, Clatke, Gilkcnson, and Capt. Whitney, as a deputation from the governor, arrived at Niagara at 7 o'clock on Wednesday morning and left again at 12 with 95 volunteers, under the command of Sheriff Hamilton, accompanied by Daniel Mc'Dougal, Esq. late of the line. They arrived almost at the same time with the men _ » of Gore, amid the cheers of the assembled thousands from the wharves. They marched up in front of the City Hall, were reviewed, and inarched to the Parliament buildings, where they received their arms and accoutrements, and ten rounds of ammunition each. Companies of men from Oakville, Whitby Scarborough, and other neighbouring towns, were continually arriving, and, on Thursday morning, upwards of foui thousand stand of aims had been given out. The troops intended to go !n search of the rebels, and, consisting of about 2,000 men, having all been marshalled, and reviewed by the governor, were led out, about ten o'clock, by liiin in person, up Yonge street, where, it was said, the rebels, in force, were wailing for us. and with whom we came up, at about 12 o'clock, at Montgomery's tavern, their head quarters. Tliey there appeared to be in considerable

numbers, amounting to between five and seven hundred men ; but from their ill chosen position, it was soon evident they could not make any effectual resistance ; and upon several shots being fired uporn tliem from two small brass field pieces, they left the house and the road þÿ a part of them taking up a position in the woods on our left, the others retreating back and to our right. Our first company, consisting of old soldiers, were immediately sent to dislodge the enemy from the wood, which tlicy did, in gallant style, in about fifteen minutes, killing about thirty, and wounding and taking prisoners a proportionable number. We followed them about two miles þÿ but Mackenzie and a greater number ol his party got off" bv scattering and taking to the woods ; and from our want of a sufficient number of cavalry, it was thought useless to follow them, they being completely, and, for the peace of society, it is to be hoped, effectually routed. We were ordered back to the city, where we arrived about 5 o'clock, amid the warm congratulations and joyful acclamation of tiie population, who consider themselves now free from any farther molestation from Mr. M ackenzie, and his murderous a?id luwlest gang. Niagara volunteers, (of which I was one,) having left home, many of tlicm without an hour's warning, and quite unprovided in purse or otherwise, and alarmed for the safely of their own homes, (for among other reports, it was said two hundred men were coining from Buffalo to take the place, desir-

ed and obtained leave from bis Excellency to return, which they did, per Transit, of yesterday morning, greeted by their friends and several hundred of the militia, who were preparing to leave with the 8. B. Britannia, to join them. I need only farther add, that this movement made by Mo'Kcnzic, in the present situation of the province, is considered by ali

garlics as a mad attempt, and that Mc'Ivenzic must have been, to a certain extent, deranged, in- with his acknowledged shrewdness lie could not but have foreseen the fatal termination of his foolish attempt to overturn the government, as it is supported by the greater number, and possessed of most effectual means to put down sedition in any part tif the province Long have Mc'Kenzie and a few such men as are to be found in any community, agitated and disturbed the country, and complained of grievances which nobody saw or felt, and even enlisted the general sympathy of the people of the United States, by praising their government, and the excellency of their institutions, (which nobody will deny,) holding our government up to scorn as oppressive, and raising the cry of Liberty ! Liberty ! But I trust his deeds for the last few days will withdraw the veil that has blinded people's eyes, and discover him in his proper colors. What more liberty do we want in Canada as a British province ? But if we want more, heaven preserve us from such liberty as we should gain by cold blooded murder þÿ (Col. Moodie was murdered last Monday, in cold blood, because he refused, it is said, to lead on- the insurgents) þÿ or hv burning our houses, robbing the mail and individuals, and such other like actions as Mo'Kunzie and his party have been guilty of. I. S. Every thing was quiet when I left Toronto except the bustle caused by the continued arrival of militia and volunteers, who

wepe hailed with pleasure, not that they were expected to be needed, but because of the loyalty and attachment to the government, their ready otfer of assistahce evinced. 1 remain, gentlemen, your obedient servant, ANGUS M'LEOD. STILL LATER þÿ 5, I'. M. The cars have just arrived. There is nothing farther from Toronto. People are in arms on both sides of the river. The ferry boats arc either entirely slopped, or all passengers strictly examined.

martial law. There can he little doubt that the power given to the commander of the forces to execute martial law in the district of Montreal, will be acted upon so long as the resistance to the civil authority continues. This is the third time that we have had martial law in Canada, under the British Government ; first, immediately after the conquest in 1759 and 1700 ; next, during the American revolutionary war in 1775-0, and now. Martial law in this province, exercised by those who derive their authority from the British crown, is not liable to the abuses with which it is accompanied in independent states; the South American republics for example. We are dependent and so are those who govern us. They are responsible in the courts of law in England, where the highest of the King's subjects are liable to impeachment and trial before an independent and enlightened tribunal. To Correspondents þÿ Under present circumstances, we have come to the determination to lay aside, for a time, the favors of our numerous correspondents who treat of the management of public affairs. The press has done much to produce the unfriendly feelings which unfortunately prevail in this province, and now favor rebellion. Those whose duty it is to put an end to it, had better, in our opinion, be left to their responsibility, free from the effect of publications which may spread suspicions ami divisions, and weaken authority. This is the course which was followed by this Gazette, during the last American war-
at a period far less difficult than the present, and we shall adhere to it till the rebellion is put down, which we trust will not be long. A very judicious resolution. þÿ Com. Adv.

It is with extreme regret I perceive the American papers along the frontier and some of your city, giving currency to the grossest misrepresentation, and favoring the cause of the French Canadian insurgents Rest assured that people are anti-reformers in every respect, actuated only by their hatred of the Anglo-Saxan race and equally the enemies of the English and Americans. The British party has been laboring to introduce register oliices and improvements on a grand scale, and to do away with the odious feudal tenure which disgraces our statutes. These objects are opposed by the French Canadians, who seek only the expulsion and destruction of the English population, in the vain hope of establishing a French republic. I may add that our cause is the cause of truth."

The following from a Baltimore paper is worthy of note : þÿ " Few persons are aware of the danger they incur by keeping lucifer matches, unless properly protected by being enclosed in an incombustible box or vessel. þÿ A circumstance strongly illustrative ot the hazardous nature of these articles occurred a short tune since in a ware room in Baltimore street. A few dozen weie put up in the usual manner, and deposited on a shelf in the vicinity of other goods, and a few days only had elapsad wiien the peculiar odour omitted by the match when burning attracted attention. On examination a box of them was found to be ignited, and the only means of safety was to get the whole lot out of the premises. No apparent cause existed for the combustion, and it occurred a few hours later, when the rooms would have been closed for night, the probability is that the whole interior of the store would have been in flames ere discovered. þÿ It lias not been many months since a large hardware establishment in this city was endunged by the falling of a box containing a few gross of these matches, from the second to the first floor of the house. The effects of the full ignited the contents of the box, which had dropped among some straw used for packing ; and although prompt exertions were used by the spectators it was with great difficulty that the burning mass could be thrown trom the store, and the straw prevented trom being consumed.

©&W&3R From t he New York Advertiser, Dec. 15. TWENTY-FIFTH CONGRESS. SECOND SESSION. IN-SENATE. Monday's proceedings, in continuation. By Mi. TALLMADGE : the following petition from Silas M. Stilwell, of the State of New Fork, in relation to abolishing imprisonment for debt in certain cases on civil process issuing out of the courts of the United States : To the Senate and House of Representatives o f the United States in Congress assembled : Your memorialist, a citizen of New York, respectfully represents : That by a law of the State of New York, passed on the 26th day of April, 1831, it is enacted " That no person shall lie arrested or imprisoned on any civil process issuing out of any court of law, or on any execution issuing out of any court of equity, in any suit or proceeding instituted for the recovery of any money due upon any judgment or decree founded upon contract, or due upon any contract express or implied, or for the recovery of any damages for the nonperformance ol any contract " By this law the State of New York has asserted the rights ot her citizens, and deprived the State courts of the power to order an arrest for debt. Notwithstanding this unequivocal expression of opinion, the United States courts still continue to infringe upon the personal liberty of the free people of this state, by causing them to be arrested upon allegations of debt. An anomaly is thus presented, of a court exercising powers of the most oppressive character, within the limits of a sovereign state, in direct violation of its expressed will

and for the exclusive benefit of the residents of other states. It is unnecessary and would be improper to address an argument to so enlightened a body, to prove the impolicy and injustice of laws which subject the liberty of one citizen to the malice and caprice of another, without requiring an allegation that an offence against the majesty of the laws has been or will be committed. And it is equally unnecessary to assert that every sovereign state should be permitted to possess laws, for the administration of justice, which shall bear equally upon ail its citizens. Believing that Congress will not intentionally inflict an injury upon any member of the Union, and being convinced that the grievance here presented is of great magnitude, and can be easily removed, your memorialist would respectfully request that the laws be so amended as to require the United States court to conform, in all civil suits, to the laws of the state in which they are located, or that the said courts, in all the states, be prohibited from issuing process to arrest or imprison for debt. Your petitioner will ever, &c. SILAS M. STILWELL. Mr. T. said that, in presenting this petition, he felt it due to the occasion to say that the petitioner was a gentleman of high standing and character in the city of New York No one in the Union had probably, given more consideration to the subject of abolishing imprisonment for debt than he, lie was for several years a distinguished member of the New York Legislature, and in 1831 succeed
ed, bv his untiring exertions, in carrying through that body the bill to abolish imprisonment for debt' in that state. Since the pas-

sage of that act, no person can be arrested or imprisoned for any debt founded upon contract, by any process issuing out of the courts of the state of New York. Still her citizens are liable to be arrested and imprisoned on ciwl process issuing out of the courts of the United States, notwithstanding that the people of the state have, in their sovereign capacity, declared it the relic of a barbarous age. M any of her citizens are now suffering imprisonment under the laws of the United States, which they could not be subjected to by the laws of the State. The laws of the State, too, are, in some cases, virtually abrogated. A creditor, in order to subject his debtor to imprisonment, has merely to take up his temporary residence in an adjoining State, and thus avail himself of the process of the courts of the United States to accomplish a purpose which he could not do as a resident, of the State. Mr. T. said he was informed that there were many cases of this description, where the law of the State is thus evaded, and cases, too, of extreme hardship. Aside from this, Mr. T. said he thought imprisonment for debt wrong in principle, and that it ought to be abolished by the United States, so far as related to civil process of their own courts. At all events, that their process should be made to conform, in this respect, to the laws of the State where imprisonment for debt is abolished. Thus much the petitioner asks, if Congress is unwilling to go farther.

The Entertainment Committee assembled yesterday morning at eight o'clock, before which hour their indefatigable chairman was at his post to make regulations about the distribution of tickets of their fellow citizens to view the hall. To form an idea, however, of the magnificent appearance of the building without the display of the fyt of gas lightning would be impossible. Indeed, the hall by day light has hut a dull and heavy appearance. Those who are desirous to see it in a state of brilliancy resembling the memorable Oth of November, must wait for the polish bail which will take place on the'2lst instant, when a comparison may lie fairly instituted. It may be proper, en passant, to state that the apprehensions entertained by some of the

fashionable families of the west end of the town, as to an issue of tickets more extensive than may be consistent with the comforts of the visitors, are quite erroneous. The issue is limited ; and Mr Peacock, the chairman of the Committee, is willing to be responsible for the slightest inconvenience of the company. It is but just to take particular notice of the gas lighting of Guildhall. Since the memorable day when so many crowned heads did honour to this ancient and noble hall, by partaking of a civic welcome, there has been no attempt till now of eclipsing the vast splendour then, for the first time displayed by gas illumination. In order to accomplish this in the fullest manner, the committee determined to spare no expense, took time bv the forelock, and began to sound the note of preparation so far back as the middle of August, when they intrusted the supervision of the department to the engineer of the Chartered Gas Company, who reported on the defective state of the old gas fittings, and a renovation attended with considerable expense took place. The chief addition made by the committee this year consists of chandeliers, constructed from the classically elegant designs and under the tasteful eye of Collins. They augment in no small degree the hitherto fascinating brilliancy of the ball. Between the panticls of painted glass which compose the body of these gigantic lamps are placed most scientifically some hundreds of glass prisms, which by their refractive power decompose

the rays of light into showers of rainbow illusion. The chandeliers were I placed Irish O enough to prevent any interference in the line of sight between the royal table and the brilliant display of gas made at t lie west end of the hall, where the star shone with its wonted effulgence from 1,505 gas lights encircled with the motto of "God save the Queen " The number of burners in these two devices (the star and motto) arc 4,500, and the weight of cut gwss is nearly one ton,
